speechtext:
I rise to direct the atten-
Privilege-Mr. Bennett

lion of the right hon. the Prime Minister {Mr. Mackenzie King), not as leader of the government but as leader of the House of Commons, to what I conceive to be a breach of one of the privileges of the house in connection with an answer made to a question asked on February 3 last by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). The hon. member asked certain questions in connection with an agreement connected with wheat, and the answer was this:
1,	2, 3. The subject to which this question relates, namely, the marketing of Canadian grains abroad, is now being investigated by the royal grain inquiry commission, which has not yet reported to the government.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that an answer such as this is not quite in accordance with the rights of parliament, because the question was as to an agreement about which there was some knowledge, and had nothing whatever to do with this royal commission, which may or may not see the agreement. As the commissioner is now engaged in dealing with textile matters, one cannot think that parliament should be put in this position. I would have mentioned it before, but I conceived it to be a matter to be dealt with only by the leader of the house. If any ordinary minister were to undertake to answer questions in this way and the right hon. gentleman were affected he would have something to say much more caustic than the observations which I now make.

Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act so as to constitute committees instead of one advisory committee, and to appropriate the necessary moneys for the continuance and extension of the work under the act for the fiscal years 1937-38 and 1939-40.
He said:	In moving that this resolution
go to the committee of the whole I should like to make a brief explanation. Dealing with the matter of committees I may remind the house that in the act passed in 1935 provision was made for the setting up of an advisory committee. The membership of that committee was indicated, not in its personnel but in regard to the organizations which were to be represented on it. We have had certain experiences during the last two years in connection with the carrying on of the work in the different provinces which indicate that it would be desirable to have authority to appoint more than one advisory committee. This particular committee which is provided for in the act as it stands will not necessarily be done away with.
It was provided in another section of the act that an amount limited to a million dollars a year could be expended in the years 1936-37, 1937-38 and 1938-39. By the amendment we are removing that limitation. I may say that I will be prepared, either in committee on the resolution or in committee after the second reading of the bill itself, to give complete information with regard to expenditures.
At this stage I would only wish to add that the total amount spent up to date in the two years is a little over 8800,000. It is not thought wise to leave the limitation in the bill as at present because of the fact that many undertakings have to be refused consideration on the ground that there may not be sufficient money available, and we think the government can give consideration to the facts in each case to better advantage if that limitation is not there.

Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Government Harbours and Piers Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I stated during the discussion of the resolution, the proposed amendments to the Government Harbours and Piers Act are desired primarily to meet changes in wharf and transportation requirements that have taken place since the act was last amended, but particularly on account of the provisions of the Consolidated Audit and Revenue Act, which requires that all the revenue of Canada shall be paid into the consolidated revenue fund. The act involves no change in practice as far as the department is concerned. The change contemplated under this amendment is exactly the practice which has been followed for many years, but conditions have 
changed over the years, and these are minor amendments which are designed to bring the act up to date.

Before second reading is given, Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my opposition to this bill in its present form, because it proposes to perpetuate a form of taxation which in its application to the smaller communities is unjust and shows unfair discrimination. I would not take up the time of the house but for the fact that I have brought the matter before the minister and the officials of his department on several- occasions, and to my dismay they have expressed renewed determination to continue this system of collecting tolls and duties, leaving without redress the smaller communities, who have suffered in some degree because of the- methods employed in the past.
I wish to make it clear that I am dealing solely with the smaller communities, whose only contact with outside civilization or with the industrial centres on which they must depend for supplies and to which they must ship their produce is over the government wharf. In the tolls that have been charged under this act the people in these communities have been penalized in their endeavour to face pioneer conditions, encouraged as they have been to leave the cities and face the inconvenience of life as found at some points along the coast. My plea is for the residents of these smaller communities. They are taxed, as all citizens are, for highways, but they have no access to our highway system. They are taxed for various public works, but it is seldom that the}' have an opportunity to enjoy the facilities provided in this regard by this dominion. Citizens who reside on the inland waters and canals of the country, for instance, and who use the wharves there located, are not taxed to the same degree, even though they have access to our highway and railway systems. They are not required to pay an additional toll for the privilege of importing necessary commodities or exporting their produce.
To show the impracticability of the present system of taxation under this bill I would refer to the returns requested by me last session. They indicate that during the fiscal year 1984-35 the total revenue secured from the collection of top wharfage was $92,096.71. For the fiscal year 1935-36 the total revenue secured from that source was $87,951.29. Out of the total revenue the commission paid to wharfingers in 1934-35 amounted to $24,862.91 and in the subsequent fiscal year to $26,034.91. That is, in 1935-36 from the imposition of top wharfage tolls the net amount was $41,916.38.

Harbours and Piers Act-Mr. MacNeil
May I point out that out of about 900 government wharves within the jurisdiction of the act, during the fiscal year 1934-35 these tolls were collected on only some 216. During the fiscal year 1935-36 they were collected on only 220. I find upon inquiry that, for reasons which I have not been able to discover, there is frequently some delay in reporting to the Department of Transport, wharves constructed at public expense by the Department of Public Works; consequently not all these wharves are listed for the appointment of wharfingers or for the imposition of tolls. Only a small number of wharfingers are appointed and tolls imposed at such wharves listed with the Department of Transport, and I believe only a comparatively small number are so listed.
There is a reason for this, and I should like to direct the attention of the government to the matter at this time, because of the unfair discrimination. It is becoming increasingly difficult to secure wharfingers. The reason is obvious. The imposition of taxation in this form is extremely inconvenient to the residents in a small community. I believe the wharfinger is allowed fifty percent of the first $200 in tolls collected, and fifteen per cent of the tolls collected thereafter. He receives no other remuneration, and is not required to perform any definite service to the public. He is not required even to take a line when a steamer docks. So far as I can learn he is not required to afford proper protection to the commodities which pass under his charge. To illustrate the discrimination I shall refer hon. members to a specific instance which came to my notice, namely that of the appointment of a wharfinger last season at Robert's Creek, British Columbia. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister at the time, pointing out that most unfair discrimination had resulted. Robert's Creek is situated only a few miles north of another wharf at Gibsons Landing. No wharfinger has been appointed at Gibsons Landing and no tolls have been collected in that community. After all, as it stands the power of appointment within the act is permissive. Immediately upon the appointment of the wharfinger the collection of tolls become mandatory. The appointee was selected for no other reason, I believe, than that he had been a faithful follower of the Liberal party, and his appointment caused grave discontent in the community. As a matter of fact at one time I thought there would be a repetition of the Boston tea party.
As the situation developed the people of the community felt that their only recourse was to make it so extremely inconvenient
for the wharfinger that he might have to discontinue his duties. That was a most unfortunate situation, and one which I believe is not at all in the public interest. The two communities are connected by a road, and one can readily understand the feeling of the residents affected by the toll. Small storekeepers in that community, as compared with the storekeepers in the south, were penalized unfairly and discriminated against with consequent diversion of business. The residents of the community, many of whom are on relief, are required to pay the toll on every small shipment of assorted groceries. Although the amount charged may be exceedingly small, it amounts to no little inconvenience and hardship to people in straitened circumstances who are now suffering very definite distress. The dairy ranchers in the community who import or ship produce are unfairly penalized. True, supplies for fishing vessels and gear are exempt, nevertheless the supplies required by families of fishermen resident in the community are subject to the imposition of these tolls.
Under the act power is given to impose the collection of side wharfage tolls. That is, it is presumed that every steamship docking at a government wharf is required to pay a toll amounting to about 50 cents. However, steamship companies enjoy the privilege of a commutation rate, and on making inquiry at the department I find that the Union Steamship Company, plying between these points on the Pacific coast, and enjoying a subvention of $18,000 annually, does not pay side wharfage tolls at Robert's Creek. Consequently we have the situation under which the residents pay top wharfage tolls and the steamship company, already generously subsidized from the federal treasury, does not pay side wharfage. Upon inquiry I find they pay tolls only at two wharves in that district, *namely at Irvines Landing and Gibsons Landing, and even at these points they enjoy a commutation rate of something like $5 per month.
I have in mind another wharf considerably north of the points in question, where every hour of every working day one can hear the rumble of the wheels of trucks connected with an industry transshipping logs for the export trade. No attempt is made at that point to levy tolls on an industry far more capable of paying them than are the residents in the community I have mentioned.
I consider the situation unbusinesslike and unfair. No stipulated remuneration is indicated, and the wharfingers have no definite responsibility to render a service to the public.
640	COMMONS
Harbours and Piers Act-Mr. Bennett
The residents in the community in question pay not only top wharfage toll, but also side wharfage, whether or not it is collected. That toll is incorporated in the freight and express charges levied upon goods carried by the steamship company. They also pay their portion of any tolls which may be collected on goods going in or out of the port of Vancouver. As a matter of fact, when these tolls are added to the prices paid in the small communities I believe it is not unfair to say that tolls are collected three or four times over, and that they constitute an additional imposition and penalty upon people who can ill afford to bear that burden. I repeat that in comparison with other citizens of the dominion these people are discriminated against.
Before the bill reaches the committee stage I would urge upon the minister that he give some assurance of an amendment which would exempt from the imposition and collection of tolls these smaller communities entirely dependent upon traffic which passes over the government wharves serving them. In a measure larger than 'heretofore I suggest that for the construction and maintenance of wharves the government should rely for _ reimbursement upon the collection of side wharfage tolls. No steps should be taken to collect more than side wharfage tolls, because after all they are passed on to the consumers resident in the district. I see no reason why the poorer sections should pay tolls twice over.
May I point out further that it is not within the range of practicability to appoint wharfingers at all these wharves. Public sentiment is definitely against such appointments. As I have pointed out, their appointment occasions grave inconvenience, and only too frequently the situation becomes so unpleasant that the official appointed is compelled to resign. Frequently those offered this unpleasant work refuse to accept it at the remuneration stipulated. The wharfingers collect commissions in very small amounts from small assortments of groceries and other small shipments. It would be a better policy if the government attempted to collect side wharfage tolls, which could be accomplished more easily and in a more businesslike way. The collections could be made at a lesser expense at the head office of the steamship companies serving the communities.
I strongly commend the matter to the consideration of the government, in order that we may not by the second reading of this bill perpetuate an unsound, unfair and unjust principle of taxation which in its application results in grave discrimination.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill embodies an amendiment to a statute, and it cannot be said to express any particular principle, apart from the one to which the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. MacNeil) has referred1. However, there is another matter of some importance which I think may be discussed in committee. I refer 'to the question of appointments. The old statute provided that these were to be made by the governor in council; the new bill provides that they are to be made by the minister, but that the salary is still to be fixed by the governor in council. To this extent there is a complete change in the principle embodied in the old statute. I do not desire to take up the time of the house in dealing with the matter at this time, other than to say that the adoption of the motion for second reading must not be taken as agreement to every point in the bill. Our rights, such as they are, to discuss the matters involved in the various sections when the house is in committee we reserve at this time in order that the bill may be expedited in its passage.

Mr. Speaker, I assume that when the minister closes the debate he will deal with the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). I think the hon. member has a misconception of the situation. He refers to the imposition of wharfage charges on these government wharves as taxation. I consider such charges to be payment for services rendered. The hon. member referred to the imposition of this taxation upon the people in these small places, but he went on to say that out of 900 wharves owned by the government, these charges were made at only 220. He stated that the wharfinger gets 70 per cent of the fees, but I believe he gets only 50 per cent up to $200, and 15 per cent after that. The hon. member said that the wharfinger rendered no services for these fees, but I think he does render a distinct service.
The wharfinger checks the freight into a shed which is kept under lock and key. When the countryman or fisherman comes along and asks for his goods, there is a guarantee that they are there, that they have not been stolen or tampered with in any way. The wharfinger checks the unloading and hands out the freight upon the production of the bill of lading. The fisherman is assured that he gets the stuff for which he has paid. If this freight were left on an open wharf with no one to take care of it, the first person who came along might take something be-

Harbours and Piers Act-Mr. Neill
longing to someone else. The freight might get wet or the crows might destroy part of it. If I were living in one of these small communities I would infinitely prefer to pay the ridiculously small charge made in order to have guaranteed protection for my goods. The steamer arrives at many of these points at very uncertain intervals, and if there was no wharfinger it would mean the people would have to remain five or six hours waiting for the boat in order to take delivery themselves. I think the services rendered are worth far more than the charge made.

Many of the wharves
have no shed.

Many of them have no sheds; the freight is left in the open, and the crows can destroy a sack of com in a very short time. The sea gulls are not altogether innocent in this regard. I believe the great majority of the wharves do have small sheds into which the freight can be put if only to protect it from the rain.
The hon. member suggests that side wharfage should be charged and collected from the steamer. Such a practice would substantially increase the expense to these people on whose behalf he is arguing. If side wharfage is collected from the steamer it will mean that these fishermen will have to pay considerably more for their goods. The steamers will certainly either increase their rates or add the charge to the customer's bill.
There is a schedule of rates fixed by government regulation, and anyone who looks at them can see how ridiculously low they are. The charges average not more than ten or fifteen cents per ton, and the wharfinger gets fifty per cent. After waiting three or four hours for a boat to come in, he meets it sometimes in the middle of the night and checks off perhaps two tons of freight. There are many places at which these steamers call where even less than that is delivered. He checks in the freight and he goes home. The next day somebody comes along and wants 200 pounds of freight. The charges might be ten cents, of which the wharfinger's share would be five cents. He may have to walk a mile to the wharf from his home if he does not happen to live right on the wharf. Tom Jones who receives a small shipment has a guarantee that his goods are protected. The wharfinger gets five cents commission. He walks home again and shortly afterwards Mrs. Smith comes along and wants a crate of chickens, on which the charges are eight cents, the wharfinger getting four. The charges are very reasonable when compared to the services rendered. The 31111-41
charges on privately owned wharves are two, [DOT]three, four and sometimes five times as much as those on the government wharves.
The hon. member declared there was discrimination due to the fact that on one wharf there will be a wharfinger while on another one a few miles away there will be none. That state of affairs is not brought about by political pressure or instigation; it is simply due to the fact that no one will take on the position of wharfinger at that particular wharf. When a man is asked to take over the job he will reply that he cannot do it for the remuneration offered. This is what has happened at many wharves, and the result is that they remain without wharfingers and consequently without collection of wharfage.
The Department of Public Works build these wharves and then turn them over to the Department of Marine for operation. The hon. member for Vancouver North said he did not know why, and I do not know why, there is very often an interval between the time the wharf is built by the Department of Public Works and the time it is handed over to the Department of Marine. I have noticed this before but I have never felt inclined to kick about it. I have always considered that the wharf was better looked after by the Department of Public Works than it would be when handed over to the Department of Marine. Since the present minister took charge of the department he has sent out notices, I suppose of a general character, to all these places to the effect that he wants a wharfinger appointed. At times I have tried to get someone to take the position of wharfinger, but no matter who I asked or what his politics were, I have been unable to do so. In one or two places I have been told that the public preferred not to have wharfingers. They make a sort of day of it and go down to meet the steamers to get what freight is coming in. The great difficulty has been to get men to accept these positions.
I do not think the general public is discriminated against because of the charges made. I am quite sure that if I lived in one of these places I would be only too glad to pay the small wharfage charges in return for the services rendered. I repeat that it is not a question of taxation; it is a question of payment for services rendered, and these are out of all proportion to the revenue obtained. That is the trouble; you cannot get anyone at the revenue provided by the government. I think the government ought to give the wharfinger all he collects up to, say, $200 a year. I have no doubt the minister will deal with the matter when he replies.

Harbours and Piers Act

Hon,. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport): Mr. Speaker, the address of the hon. member , for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has shortened mine considerably. A statement was made which I should correct, that no wharfage is charged on inland waters. That is entirely erroneous. Such docks as are built by the Public Works department and turned over to Transport for operation are provided with wharfingers where possible and exactly the same scale of fees is charged as on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. There are certain docks along the canals, and these charge a somewhat higher scale of wharfage. The revenues are taken into the canal accounts rather than into the accounts we are considering here.
The figures given by my hon. friend from Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) do not agree with mine. According to my figures there are 94S wharves under the management of the department, of which 381 have wharfingers and 567 have not. The gross collections for 19351936, that is, in respect of both side and top wharfage, were $146,697.07, while the amount retained from that as remuneration for the wharfingers was $26,034.94, leaving a net revenue to the department of about $120,000. Of the 381 wharves having wharfingers, only 282 yield revenue. For the remainder a wharfinger is appointed who makes his reports, but the reports indicate that there is no movement over the dock. Of the number yielding revenue only fifty-one yield $500 gross each; twenty-nine yield over $1,000 gross, and one wharf yields up to $15,000.
As for the abolition of wharfingers, I think that would be a backward step. Many of the docks require services other than just the tying up of ships and the counting of cargoes. Many of the docks have sheds used for various purposes, and of which the wharfinger is custodian. We have, for instance, potato wharves, some of them heated; many wharves have lights, and it would be quite impossible to operate lights for the dock unless someone is responsible.
I think it is a great pity to stir up feeling against the collection of wharfage at any point. Every town that asks for the accommodation of a public dock should) have enough public spirit to fall in with the appointment of a wharfinger and pay the trifling fees that are charged for the service. In fact I think each dock should have a wharfinger, whether there is any business there or not. If the government builds a dock at that point, someone should be responsible. We should) have the benefit at head office of reports from the locality indicating what repairs are necessary; and, where the traffic warrants, the dock

should be lighted, and someone should be responsible for the lights.
The suggestion was made that side wharfage should be charged and top wharfage eliminated), and that side wharfage should be collected at head office from the steamship companies. That could be done, although it would be simply substituting an indirect tax for a direct tax on the user of the docks, and probably the indirect tax would be much higher than any direct tax paid through a wharfinger. The difficulty in that method of collection is that we would have no one at the dock responsible for the operation andl condition of the dock, which is very important. Under all the circumstances, therefore, I believe the present system meets the case better than any other that has been suggested to-day.

On section 3-Appointment of officers and employees.

In view of the discussion on the second reading I should like further information from the minister as to what instructions are given to the wharfingers. There seems to be some misunderstanding, because in the district I represent I have had no evidence that wharfingers are required: to render service to the public of the kind to which reference was made by my hon, friend from Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). There is a haphazard performance of their duties. They do not assist in taking lines from vessels or share any responsibility for the care and protection of goods that are landed on the wharf. In the district to which I refer
31111-41J
very seldom do vessels bring in goods to any considerable quantity except during daylight hours.

The wharfinger has a general supervision of the dock. He is not necessarily a warehouse man. He does not assume financial responsibility for the goods that are put on the dock, though he has instructions to see that they are properly taken care of and distributed. He collects the fees at the dock, looks after the dock in a general way, takes care of the lighting if there is any, and so on.

I may remark in passing
that at the wharves I speak of there are no lights except such as the residents provide. In what manner are these appointments made?

They are made by the minister. The recommendations come from the member for the district or from the department's agency, in case the member is not able to nominate a wharfinger. We use every means at our disposal to get a man who is willing to act. The difficulty is to get men. I have some 500 letters outstanding asking for wharfingers, and have not been able to get satisfactory replies. The treasury have men checking up as well because they must look after the interests of the treasury.

Why can men not be
obtained?
Mr. HOWE':	For the reason stated a
moment ago. There is some little agitation worked up at local points; they may decide that they will not have a wharfinger, and if one is appointed he is not allowed to act. It is a local revolution, and I hope that hon. members will have nothing to do with one.

I can assure the minister
that if there is any local revolution I have nothing to do with it. I want to draw his attention to three wharves within a few miles of one another connected by road-Gibsons Landing, Robert's Creek and Wilson's Creek. These wharves were constructed and are maintained at the public expense. No top-wharfage tolls are collected, but side wharfage tolls are collected at Gibsons Landing. At Robert's Creek a wharf constructed a number of years ago and which was recently transferred to the Transport department, the wharfinger was appointed last season. The minister can understand the resentment that arises in a community, when after they have been shipping produce for a number of years without paying any toll, to have- one suddenly imposed upon them at a time when hardship is bound to ensue. Immediately
Harbours and Piers Act

north is Wilson's Creek and as far as I have been able to discover that has not yet been transferred to the department. Those who enjoy the facilities established at public expense at that point pay no toll.
The hon. member for [DOT]Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) referred to the collection of side-wharfage dues. The rate is set by regulation under the act, and I believe it is something like 50 cents per call for vessels of the size that make use of these wharves, vessels under 500 tons. In the fixing of freight and express charges on goods moving back and forth, the side wharfage charges are taken into the calculation, and the residents must pay the side wharfage due in such case whether it is actually collected by the government or not at any of these points. On what basis this is computed in the carriage rates I am not sure. In view of the circumstance I have brought to the minister's attention, I should appreciate some suggestion from him as to how this obviously unfair discrimination might be eliminated. Even if it is extremely difficult to appoint wharfingers some other scheme might be devised so that one particular community might not be singled out while others escape the payment of the toll. The imposition of this tax on the smaller communities is quite unnecessary. The people do not enjoy the services which one would regard as only reasonable in view of the charges collected, and they suffer many inconveniences in addition. I suggest that the residents of these places should be encouraged to stay there instead of being discouraged by the government. Has the minister any suggestion as to how this unfair discrimination might be removed?

My hon. friend has referred ;o Gibsons Landing, which is perhaps a fair example of many of these wharves. In 1928 there was considerable correspondence in an effort to obtain a wharfinger for that point, but without success. The effort was renewed in 1930, again without success, and in 1931 there was again a good deal of correspondence. Efforts were made again at the end of 1935 and early in 1936 and we are still unable to get a wharfinger. I understand that this place is in the hon. gentleman's constituency and if he is willing to look into the matter and suggest a name for wharfinger, we will be delighted to appoint him.

Can the minister tell us why side wharfage tolls are not collected at all points and levied against the steamship company? I would point out to him that in these districts I have1 mentioned side wharfage dues are paid only at Irvine's Landing and

Gibsons Landing. At Robert's Creek, although top wharfage tolls are collected, side wharfage tolls are not.
At what points at West Kootenay, along the Arrow lakes and Kootenay lake, are there wharfingers?

AVith regard to the question asked by my hon. friend (Mr. MacNeil), the wharfinger should collect side wharfage tolls at all points. If he collects at some and not at others he is negligent. The act provides that the minister may commute wharfage with steamship companies by paying them a lump sum for the season or per month through the head office by arrangement with the department, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that there is no attempt at evasion. As regards the question asked by my hon. friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) I understand that he wishes to know at what points on the Arrow lakes there are wharfingers. The following wharves are on interior lakes. I am not quite familiar with the geography: Naramata,, Peachland, Penticton and Sum-merland appear on the list as having wharfingers.

This seems to be the only clause in this bill of any great importance and I should like the minister to explain why he is suggesting this change, which is a rather serious one. Under the present law all the employees are appointed by the governor in council. It is quite true that the recommendations for appointments have always been made by the minister, but the onus of making the appointments rests with the government as a whole. In this clause the minister is asking that he shall be given the sole authority to make appointments without going to the governor in council. What possible reason is there for making such a change?

This practice goes back to 1923. Prior to that it was a duty of the civil service commission, and prior to that, when this act was drafted, it was done by the governor in council. The civil service commission found it absolutely impracticable to handle these appointments, probably because it is so difficult to get anyone to act. In 1923 an amendment was passed to the Civil Service Act excepting these appointments from the operation of the act and placing them under the minister. I do not know why it should be under the minister rather than the governor in council, except that the transactions are so small that it seems hardly worth while cluttering up the minutes of council with them.

The council fixes the
salaries.
It approves the remuneration.
They are determined.
Yes, the regulations are determined by order in council.

I do not think the minister has given any good reason for the change. After all, this is the only clause of any importance in the bill. I quite agree that the civil service commission could not make these appointments satisfactorily, and I think the change was properly made giving the authority to the governor in council. But now the minister himself is asking for authority to appoint these people. It has been my experience that the recommendation of the minister has usually been agreed to by council. There must be some reason which we do not know why the minister seeks this change. Why does he not leave it alone? I take it the bill is brought in for no other purpose than to provide for the change suggested in section 3. I for one should like some satisfactory explanation.

The present act provides that it shall be done by order in council. In 1918 the Civil Service Act provided that these appointments should be taken from the governor in council and placed in the hands of the civil service commission. In 1922 the Civil Service Act was amended to provide that these appointments should be made by the minister. That has been the practice since 1922; they are appointed by the minister by virtue of the amendment to the Civil Service Act of 1922. We are simply changing the act to conform to the existing practice. For the past fifteen years the appointments have in fact been made by the minister without reference to the governor in council, by virtue of the amendment to which I have referred.
Does the minister mean that notwithstanding the way this act reads at present the minister has been making these appointments without referring them to the governor in council?
Yes. We do it, as I say, by virtue of the amendment to the Civil Service Act of 1922.
My memory of it is that it has not been done in that way, but if the minister is certain-
It was done by the governor in council on the recommendation of the minister.
My officers assure me it is done by departmental letter, and has been done in that way since 1922. In actual practice the minister is seldom consulted about it.

That is to see if they will take the position, but I can recall orders in council appointing wharfingers. The difficulty has been to find someone willing to be ap^ pointed, but when the time for appointment came I can recall some cases at least during recent years in which the recommendation of the minister was that so and so be appointed and that the salary consist of the fees which he receives; dozens of cases of that kind come to my mind at the moment. The minister is quite right in saying that there is no reference to the minister about it. When someone has expressed willingness to act, the appointment is made in the manner indicated in the statute.

Perhaps my right hon. friend is confusing wharfingers with harbour masters. They also are paid by fees of office. My two officers, one of whom has been in the department many years, assure me that no wharfinger has been appointed by order in council since 1922.
He should know. It may be that I confuse wharfingers with harbour masters.

I think the minister will find that he is letting himself in for a lot of trouble, as far as the wharves serving small communities are concerned. Along the Arrow and Kootenay lakes there are about forty small wharves. In all my experience of forty years I have heard of only one wharfinger having been appointed in that district, and he had a rather unhappy experience. He had a consuming desire to possess a government job. He was appointed under the fee system. There happened to be an Anglican missionary parson there, and about the only real money that wharfinger ever collected was a dime. The parson was getting aboard the boat and happened to remember that he wanted to go back to the store. He left his suit case on the wharf. When he came back and took it up he was told to drop it; that it would cost him ten cents. The fact is that steamers along the Arrow lakes refuse to pay any fees; they just run the bow on the beach, throw out a plank and load or unload their freight on the beach. The communities protest against the payment of any fees. In one place they directed that their freight and express be unloaded on the wharf opposite and it would be brought over on the ferry free of charge. The wharfinger put

the freight into the shed, looked the shed, which was an unusual thing, and went home for the day. About six miles away there was a logging camp. The men came in the evening to get their week's supply of meat, and found the shed looked. They observed that there were strap hinges on the door, so they got a screw driver and took off the hinges and took their meat home. The next morning the wharfinger came down and thought that someone had been tampering with the lock, so he bought a new padlock at his own expense. The next week the same thing occurred. Then he took a logging chain and put it around the shed and through the handles of the door. Shortly afterwards the loggers came down for their meat, and they took off the logging chain, door and all, and threw it into the lake. It required an order in council to have the man appointed and an order in council to have him removed on a protest from the people at that point. So as I say, the minister will have a lot of trouble, first of all through protests against the fees, and then if it is to be a salary over and above any fees he will have a good deal of difficulty in satisfying the innumerable applicants for these posts.
I think that is one case where the minister would be wise in not appointing anyone. It would be in the interest of the clerical gentleman.
There are many communities more law-abiding than the one just described.

I understand the minister corrected the figures. I may explain that these figures were furnished on an order of the house for a return last session. I understand that of some 948 wharves there are only a limited number on which top wharfage dues are collected. I am not so much interested in the appointment of wharfingers as in the exact number of wharves where top wharfage dues are collected. May I also ask if those 948 wharves represent the total number of government wharves or only those that have been transferred to the Department of Transport? Is there any considerable number of wharves over and above that number not yet transferred from the Department of Public Works?

I may say that exactly 282 wharves yield revenue, both side and top *wharfage being collected. There are many wharves that have not been turned over to us for administration, and are still under the Department of Public Works.

In connection with the appointment of wharfingers, is it the intention of the government to appoint them for a number of years?
[Mr Esling]
They are appointed during pleasure, which usually means that they are permanent during good behaviour.
How does the department determine when a wharfinger is needed at any particular place?

We try to get wharfingers for all wharves, but that is not always possible. We have agents scattered all over the country; we get a report from our agent as to the business over the wharf, and if it is a very substantial amount we make a determined effort to secure a wharfinger. By law we are supposed to have a wharfinger for every wharf in Canada, and we make every attempt to do so.
But there is not a wharfinger for every wharf?
No.
I assume this bill has nothing to do with railway wharves?
Nothing at all.

In my county there is a
railway wharf at Lunenburg and another wharf at Bridgewater. It appears that the wharf at Bridgewater is controlled by the Department of Public Works and the wharf at Lunenburg is controlled by the railway company. There is no wharfinger at Lunenburg but there is a wharfinger at Bridgewater. I may say that the wharves which are under the control of the Department of Public Works are much better looked after than the wharves under the control of the railways; we find it much harder to get repairs from the railways. Very few of the wharves in my county have sheds on them, so that the service rendered in return for the top and side wharfage is not so apparent as it might be at other points. However, I must say that I do not think there is any attempt to collect wharfage from the small dealer who lands at the wharf; I think it is collected only from a ship with a cargo, and that sort of thing, and of course that is expected.

Section agreed to.

Should you not make it read "any other Canadian port" in line 9? We want to make it clear that we cannot claim the right to hold a ship anywhere else than in a Canadian port.
I have no objection whatever.
Of course it is implied in any case.

speechtext: This is a non-contentious item, some of the details of which have been in the estimates every year since about 1916, dealing with injuries sustained by civilians who have been working in connection with the Department of National Defence, or the widows of such who died.

Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce): This vote involves an increase of $35,083. The increase is accounted for wholly by increases in salaries.
What are they?
In the headquarters staff and in the bureau of statistics. Shall I give the increases in order?

Yes, because this raises a question which I want to discuss in some detail. There is the question of what Mr. Muir is doing, and matters of that kind. I should like to have the particulars of the increases.
As I said a moment ago, the total increase over last year is $35,083. The first increase is that of Mr. F. E. Bawden, $240.
What does he do?
Mr. Bawden is connected with the branch of the department which deals with steamship subsidies.
What is his present salary?
Mr. Bawden's present salary is $4,260, which is being increased to $4,500. His title is director of trade routes and steamship subsidies.
Would the minister prefer that we discuss this appropriation item by item as we go along, or wait until he finishes?
I believe there are officials of the department here, and I am quite prepared to deal with these matters now if it seems desirable.

We will wait until they
come, then. After the minister has made his statement we can deal with them further, when the officials are here.
Mr. ROGERS. I shall continue. Next, there is the salary of T. G. Major, transferred from Commercial Intelligence Service, $3,600; the salary of S. Cuddy, transferredi from weights and measures, $2,790. That covers the headquarters office. I no-w come to the salary changes in the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. They are these:	One statistician, grade 2,
vacant, $2,400; five clerks grade 2, at $1,080, totalling $5,400; one stenographer, grade 2,

81,080; 2 office appliance operators at 81,020, totalling $2,040; one stenographer, grade 1, $720; 18 clerks, grade 1, at $720, totalling $12,960, one office boy 8600, making a grand total of $25,240. The minister will observe that this departs from the procedure with respect to statutory increases in connection with salaries on a higher scale. I believe statutory increases amount to approximately five per cent; up to a certain point, that is the maximum. The others are cases in which special provision is made for those in the higher brackets. It would require something more than has been said to explain why that should be dbne, if it is not to be left open to the criticism that there was discrimination.
The other question I wish to raise is one which has to do with the dissemination of information. Some years ago the last government provided a publicity agent in the Department of Trade and Commerce, in the person of Mr. Muir. From information which comes to me I gather there has been some change in his position. I should like to know what his present duties are, and the kind of information he is responsible for gathering and sending abroad. I should like particular enlightenment as to the information he sends out of the country by cable and how and under what vote the bills for cables are paid.

I shall be pleased' to get
the information as soon as possible. With reference to the first point raised by the leader of the opposition, may I say that in the case of Mr. Bawden the salary increase would be fully in conformity with the five per cent.
But there is a maximum, and it exceeds the maximum.
It appears that Mr. Bawden was reclassified by the civil service commission, which accounts for his increase from $4,260 to $4,500. The other two in the headquarters staff were transferred.
I know about that.

I am informed Mr. Muir
comes under the organization of the bureau of statistics and holds the office of an editor, grade 2. I take it that any information coming from him for publicity purposes would appear in the publications of the bureau of statistics.
So would I.
I have no other information respecting the matter.

That is the point about which I was inquiring. Apparently the minister and myself have the same appreciation of the situation. I should like to know whether my information is correct. The minister will observe I was careful to say that I was informed; I do not know whether my information is accurate, but it is to the effect that Mr. Muir has been sending abroad cables in the nature of propaganda with respect to certain matters. I should like the minister to look into it and see whether he has incurred any bills for cables in the last few months. If so, out of what moneys are those bills paid, and is the bureau of statistics or the Department of Trade and Commerce responsible for them? In some instances the information is of a kind available in the department and known to the public only when given to it by the department. I believe it would be found that in some instances he has advance information with respect to matters, and makes it available by means which are denied-I think that is the proper word- to those who are responsible for the dissemination of information to the public generally. I would like the minister to look into the matter, fully realizing that he cannot answer to-day. The matter involves a question of principle which, I believe, is of some importance, which has been dealt with on more than one occasion, and concerning which the present leader of the government on more than one occasion in days past expressed very strong convictions.
I shall be pleased to look into the matter. Of course the leader of the opposition realizes I have not the information before me at this time.
Quite.

I should like to have a precise understanding of the nature of the complaint. As I understand it, the suggestion is that Mr. Muir was giving information in a capacity other than that of an editor in the bureau of statistics.

I do not know what he conceives his duty as editor to be. I was directing attention to information which had come to me, and I have asked the minister to ascertain whether that information has a foundation in fact, namely, that information has been cabled from this country at public expense. This information is in the nature of propaganda which at the time it was sent

Supply-Trade and Commerce
was not quite available to other organs of public opinion. I believe I have put it as fairly as I can.
I think I understand.

Has any thought been given in the bureau of statistics to getting information respecting trade among the provinces of the dominion? It is almost impossible to learn from the figures obtained by the bureau what constitutes trade among the provinces. Some time ago the Duncan commission made a report on their inquiry into maritime claims in which they indicated that they had experienced difficulty in making a finding with respect to trade because they had not available the statistics to which I have referred. In the report of the commission we find at page 44 the following observation:
We have had brought before us the lack of any comprehensive measurement of the trade of the maritime provinces with other provinces and with foreign markets. We were ourselves disappointed not to be able to pursue investigations on trade matters along lines which such statistics would have enabled us to do. We found on inquiry at the Dominion Bureau of Statistics that consideration had been given some time ago to this very subject but, mainly through lack of organization in the statistics relating to certain phases of transportation, it was not possible to proceed with the plans that had been formulated. We strongly urge that these difficulties should be overcome, as they can be, and that on this phase of internal trade a system of statistics should be made regularly available from as early a date as possible.
There was a recommendation made some years ago by the Duncan commission and1 I do not think any steps have been taken since then to obtain the necessary information. I appreciate the fact that the acting minister is familiar with the difficulties about which I am complaining, and I should like to know if any efforts are to be made to obtain statistics along these lines.

I shall be very glad to find out what progress has been made by the bureau of statistics in the direction suggested by my hon. friend. I can say now that there are very serious difficulties in the way of securing that information accurately. I recall some years ago trying to arrive at an approximate balance with respect to a single province, and I found that the bureau of statistics could give little more than the movement of carloadings in and out of provinces.
And by water.

And the movements by water. After all, we could not reduce those to terms of dollars and cents; it is quantities only. Much of the carloadings consist of less
than carload shipments and these could not possibly be reduced to dollars and cents. The bureau of statistics have done a very useful work in recent years in analyzing retail sales in the various provinces. I believe they have done that with a view to arriving at a more accurate measurement of internal trade than we have had hitherto. I should be surprised if the bureau felt at the present time that it could give us any assurance of being able to provide an accurate statistical summary of interprovincial trade. As a matter of fact the United States have encountered the same difficulty and have not been able to provide this information.
Is the information as to retail sales available from the bureau?

If I remember correctly, this analysis of retail sales was commenced about five years ago. It was based particularly upon the census of 1931. Since that time there have been annual corrections and breakdowns of the retail sales in the various provinces.
It is only an estimate, in the last analysis.
It does not profess to be accurate, although I believe a greater approach to accuracy is attained as the analysis is continued from year to year.

May I point out that this matter is becoming increasingly important because of the fact that some provinces now have income tax laws. Exporters in Nova Scotia have been subjected to taxes in Ontario on the profits of their trade in that province. The acting minister will see that this will disturb the balance as between a province which has an income tax and thus taxes the profit on trade from another province, and a province which has no income tax. For this reason I believe it would be very enlightening to have these statistics. We in the maritime provinces will be able to show that while we are subject to an income tax on goods going into the central provinces, we buy infinitely more from those provinces.

When the item covering the bureau of statistics is before the committee this information requested by the hon. member for Saint John (Mr. Ryan) and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) can be supplied. I have no doubt I shall be able to discover from the officials of the bureau just how far they have been able to make progress in the direction suggested, what obstacles still remain, and whether in their opinion they are insuperable.

Conciliation and Labour Act, $35,000.

This item covers the
expenditures connected with the printing and publishing of the Labour Gazette, which is the official organ of the department. It also covers the salaries of persons employed as Labour Gazette correspondents, which range from $120 to $300 per year. At present there are only forty-three of these correspondents employed by the department. The item provides also for special work on rental and wage surveys, in providing statistics and for conciliation in labour disputes. I may say that it has been found desirable to make full use of the conciliation branch of the Department of Labour. Instead of encouraging the setting up of conciliation boards, it has been found that a conciliation officer from the department is often able to effect the same results at considerably less expense.

Could the minister
indicate what changes have been made in the correspondents during the last year? I had one communication in connection with this matter.
I have before me a complete list of the correspondents but I have not a statement of the replacements. I can assure the leader of the opposition that there have been very few replacements.
I thought perhaps the minister could tell me what the changes were and why.

I shall have to speak from memory on this matter, but my distinct impression is that the changes made were due either to death or to retirement or, in certain cases, to the reinstatement of correspondents who appear to have been dismissed in 1930 or thereabouts. But there were very few cases of that kind.
There are only forty-three altogether.
To the best of my recollection there have not been more than half a dozen changes in the past year.

Perhaps the minister
would ascertain at what points changes have been made.
Would this item cover the expenses of the board which recently considered the dispute between the two railway companies and the men in connection with wage cuts?

That would come under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. Conciliation boards to deal with railway disputes or disputes in connection with public utility companies would be set up under that act, which is covered by another item.

Just one other question. Under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, while I cannot quote the section exactly from memory, the terminology of one section is such as to prevent, or to attempt to prevent, employers from changing hours of labour or general working conditions without reference to the employees of the particular industry affected. I wanted to bring before the house at some stage, and I ask whether this is the proper time, the question of the changing of the hours of labour and general working conditions in the Post Office Department, and to ask whether this government takes the position with reference to its own employees of being under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. I should like the opportunity to discuss this question either under this head or at some other time, because it is most important that a government enacting legislation for the guidance of employers should itself be the best sort of employer, and ought to bring itself under its own statutes with reference to its employees. If this is not the proper time to discuss the question, I shall discuss it at some future time.

Without desiring in any
way to curtail discussion on any particular point, I think it would be more appropriate if my hon. friend's question were brought up under the vote covering the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. I might remind him, however, that the government has enacted a fair wages act, which does cover the wages and hours of labour of its own employees and also of those who are engaged on government contracts.

Supply-Labour-Disputes
Perhaps under this item I might ask the minister if he can give us any information in regard to the strike at the cotton mills at Welland.

Perhaps my hon. friend will recall that last week the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Damude) directed the attention of the house to the strike at Welland and asked what progress had been made towards its settlement. I informed him at that time that a request had been received by the Department of Labour for the setting up of a board of conciliation. That request was made by the mayor of Welland on behalf of the city council, and also by the employees concerned. It was pointed out, however, that for the setting up of a board of conciliation for a dispute which did not relate to a public utility it was necessary to secure the consent of both parties to the dispute. When the hon. member for Welland put his question to me a few days ago, we were still in communication with the representatives of the company and hoped that they might see their way clear to accept a board of conciliation, but over the week-end it has developed that the company does not feel it desirable to have a board of conciliation established. At the same time they have advised us that they would welcome a conciliation officer from the Department of Labour. They have asked particularly that the chief conciliation officer should go to Welland in order to reopen negotiations for a settlement. That is the position at the present time.
I am glad to say that the employees concerned have also communicated that they would welcome the assistance of the chief conciliation officer at this time. It has been a prolonged strike of some six weeks' duration, if I remember correctly. The Department of Labour from the beginning offered its good offices in the matter, but up to the present time it has seemed to be impossible to bring the two parties together. However, in view of what has taken place in the last few days, I think we may assume that settlement has been brought nearer.

I am not criticizing anything that the department has done; for I think they have done all that is within their power to bring the parties together. But it does seem to me that the company concerned is playing for time, just in the hope that by keeping the men out longer and making their conditions more desperate they will ultimately compel them to go back on the company's own terms. I think that is a very unfortunate thing. I do not see myself why
a company, particular one enjoying all the privileges of protection which this company does, should refuse conciliation, especially when it has been requested both by the employees and by the council of the town of Welland. I do not see what difference it makes whether they have a conciliation officer or a board of conciliation. There is really little difference. Had the company accepted the board in the first place, I have no doubt that the dispute would have been amicably adjusted within a very short time, but as it is now, there is no telling how long the strike may continue or the direction in which it may develop. I am sorry that the company has adopted the attitude it has, and I had hoped that the government would have found ways and means of bringing a company of that kind to time, at least to the extent that they would deal1 directly with their own employees.

I might point out that the mere setting up of a board of conciliation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act does not of itself ensure a settlement of the dispute, because it would still be open to either party to reject the proposed basis of settlement. So that the sending of a conciliation officer to Welland may conceivably have, and I certainly hope it will have, precisely the same beneficial effect as the setting up of a board of conciliation, and possibly within a shorter space of time.
I can inform my hon. friend that the Department of Labour did hope very much that the company would see its way clear to accept a board of conciliation, particularly in view of the fact that it had been requested by the city council and by the employees. We cannot do more than urge our views upon the company concerned. It rests with the company to determine whether or not under the circumstances it will consent to the setting up of a board.

All that I was pointing out, and it is borne out I think by what the minister has just said:, is that if the company were willing to try to bring about an amicable adjustment, it would have been just as easy for them to say yes to the appointment of a -board of conciliation as to say no, and it would at least have shown a willingness on their part to do something towards bringing about the settlement which I know the department so much desires. But evidently the company have thought fit to take a different course of action, and all I can do is to hope, as does the minister, that the chief conciliation officer will be able to bring about a settlement, which is much to be desired in the interests of all concerned.

May I say a word supplementary to what has been saids by my colleague? The minister says: We cannot do more. I think the department can do more. It is only a few weeks since I chanced to be in Welland for a few hours. The strike was then on. I met a number of fairly representative citizens, and they were, so far as I could find, unanimous in wishing for a settlement and in denouncing the very low wages and the very bad: conditions that prevailed in that factory. The workers were trying to maintain order, and they were taking the only way open to them to press their claims for decent living conditions.
I received last night a telegram from the Welland textile workers strike committee, urging that this matter should be brought up in the house at an early day. They say they have done their part; they are willing to accept a board of conciliation. Indeed, they plead that a board be appointed. They refer to the very low wages and the bad conditions that have been revealed in the textile industry by the Turgeon commission.

Perhaps the minister
would state the facts so that we might have them on Hansard.

It seems to me, in view of the published facts with regard to conditions in the textile industry, and having regard to what the people in Welland call the arrogant attitude of the company in refusing to recognize the union or to accept a board appointed by the government, the state of affairs is such that it is not sufficient for the head of the Department of Labour to say, "We really cannot do anything about it."

My hon. friend is not fair in that statement. I said that we could not do more under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act applies to public utilities generally. It can be applied to other industries provided that where a dispute has occurred in such other industry both parties to the dispute consent *to the setting up of a board. When we have the abominable conditions that have been revealed to the public by the Turgeon commission-the public know all about it-I do not think we as a parliament can remain indifferent to this sort of thing. If the men riot and destroy property there is immediately a great cry and it is said that we must stand for law and order. Surely the most important duty of law and order is protection of the lives and welfare of the men, women and children of the country. In the textile industry men, women and children are being subjected to a degrading kind of life. They are not living as Canadians ought to live; it is impossible for them to live as Canadians should live. What is the use of safe-guarding law and order when we neglect the conditions that inevitably produce a breach of law and order-unless the people are content to become abject slaves. These textile workers, as far as I can gather, have proceeded in an orderly way and have been very patient. There is only one point to which I might speak, and it is one that arose in the years before 1935. Under the decision of the courts it is competent for any employer to say to a conciliation officer, "I do not want you here at all." That has been one of the difficulties which has appeared in a practical way. I wonder whether the minister has anything to say as to any further development in that connection. Perhaps the best illustration of that was found in a case some years ago in which the employer said, "I am quite capable of carrying on my own negotiations. Thank you: I do not want vou." If my appreciation of the law as it stands is correct, we have no right to say to him that he must or should do so and so. Is that still the department's appreciation of the law?

The conciliation service
operates more particularly under another statute, the Conciliation and Labour Act, which leaves it to the Minister of Labour at his own discretion to dispatch a conciliation officer to the scene of a dispute. But experience has proved that if the employer is entirely unwilling to accept the conciliation officer, to send him there may even prejudice a settlement which otherwise might be obtained. I believe actually this conciliation service of the Department of Labour is making its way through a recognition, on the part of employees and employers alike, of the fact that it can provide a very useful service in solving these disputes, and I doubt whether the matter can be dealt with upon any other basis. Compulsion is not going to induce employers or employees to accept willingly the services of a board of conciliation or a conciliation officer.
How do they do it in Australia?
I had intended to come to that point. They have worked upon a somewhat different basis there. They have what in effect are wage courts.
Not in effect; that is what they are.
They operate as wage courts, originally under state law and now, I believe, under commonwealth law.

There were two. Mr. Bruce ran one election on the theory that there should not be two and that the federal court should be preferred to the state courts. The response was not quite as general as might have been expected. There are still two courts, the state court and the commonwealth court, and the very difficulty the minister has mentioned here applies in that country as well as in New Zealand. The decision of the court is not binding as a judgment of the court and therefore, notwithstanding the decision of the court, there have been strikes or cessations of effort. The ever present difficulty is the one to which the minister has just referred. You may negotiate and arrive at what you conceive to be a reasonable arrangement. Then, after you go away, one party to the dispute may say, "Well, after all we do not think this is satisfactory," and there is no power anywhere to give finality or effect to the decision that may be reached.
Would the minister give us an idea of what value he places on these men, since apparently these matters seem to be under provincial jurisdiction?

Perhaps I may answer that in this way. The determination of wages and hours of labour would seem to fall within provincial jurisdiction, with the exception indicated as to federal public works and contracts for the federal government. But there is nothing to prevent the federal Department of Labour from offering the services of a conciliation officer to adjust any dispute whatsoever, provided the parties are willing. As a matter of fact, so far as the duties of a conciliation officer are concerned, it is not essential but it is obviously desirable that both parties be willing.
In this particular instance the one party was not prepared to accept these gentlemen.

Who are negotiators only.

organization nominate a board member; the employers nominate another member, and these two bodies try to agree on a third member who will act as chairman. In a situation of some

In my experience, conciliation officers have done good work. Even if such legislation were within the competence of the federal parliament, upon this occasion I am not going to express an opinion as to whether or not we should have compulsory conciliation or arbitration. Many observations could be made both for and against the convention. In industrial disputes usually one side or the other may not wish to negotiate. If the labourers or workers believe they have the advantage they take this position: "We have made our demands, and we are not going to discuss them." On the other hand, if the employer thinks the advantage is with him, and that he is within his rights in refusing to negotiate, he takes the same position. The conciliation officer may bring them together and point out to them that the dispute would not only affect the employer or the workers, but have social consequences as well, and in many instances he is successful in bringing the parties together. I believe every possible assistance should be given in the settlement of disputes, but it is my view that in the future the government may have to go much further than they have done in the past. In looking over the present world situation we find that in those countries where trade union movements have been generally accepted by employers and have become a part of the general life of the country, in the last few 31111-42
years labour disputes have been much less than in countries where employers have not accepted the trade union movement.
Great Britain, for example.

Yes, and the Scandinavian countries. Although in past years there have been many important strikes in Australia, despite compulsory arbitration, in the last few years it has been fairly immune from protracted strikes. I believe the government will have to give the matter further consideration than has been given in the past.

There is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. I notice that in the item fair wages *are implied. I still receive complaints in regard to wages paid on government contracts, and I am wondering to what extent the Department of Labour goes in its investigation of these matters. Complaints are not so much about contracts let directly by various departments of government as about contractors to whom the government, contractor has sublet, over which subcontracts the government may have no control. I wonder how far the Department of Labour can go toward seeing that the proper rate of pay is paid to workers on government contracts.

A schedule of wages is inserted in the specifications of all government contracts, and that specification also covers subcontracts. When a complaint is made an investigation is entered upon by the fair wage officer of the department. I believe one may say the sanction behind the discovery of any offence is the power of the government to withhold the balance of the contract price. I do not believe it is possible to have every government contract under continuous supervision. We have acted upon the principle that when there is a complaint it will be immediately investigated, and when proved, the remedy will follow.
Must there be a complaint before the department will make an investigation?

It is not necessary to have a complaint before making investigation, but on the other hand up to this time the department has not accepted the principle that we should employ enough inspectors to give continuous supervision to the performance of all government contractors.
I think there has been a good deal of confusion in connection with the fair wage stipulation in government contracts.

Not on the part of the contractor himself.



Supply-Labour-Fair Wages

It may be on tbe part of the subcontractor. I am speaking in a general way, and am not directing my remarks to any particular person who may perform government work. I do not believe the government, which has some responsibility in the matter, should wait until a complaint is received. The experience in all provinces has been that there is a tendency for employees to be afraid of submitting their complaints to union or government officials, because of the discrimination which ultimately might be exercised against such person.
Dismissal from his job.

I have known of cases in certain parts of Canada where proper wages have been entered in employers' pay-rolls, but where in fact the employers have not paid the wages prescribed by the provincial law and the terms of the contract. I do not suggest that there should be continuous supervision of the pay-roll of employers who are doing government work, but I do suggest that occasionally a fair wage officer should visit the concerns in question and examine the payrolls. Sometimes they might do well to get into contact with the officials of the union. Such action would no doubt have a salutary effect upon employers who may attempt to avoid responsibility.
Further, I have had complaints from good employers who want to pay reasonable wages as prescribed by law, or as arranged between themselves and trades unions. They complain about undercutting carried on by certain employers who are trying, by deducting from the wages of their employees, to make up the amount they have lost through a low bid. That is why I suggest to the minister the adoption of some method whereby a fair wage officer or some other employee of the department would have an opportunity of visiting these factories working on government contracts in order to see that the contracts are being lived up to.

I shall be very glad to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend. I might say that there is quite effective supervision of the larger contracts. Also the schedule of wages is posted on the premises where the work is being done and is available to the trade unions particularly affected. In the nature of things, the complaint would come to the Department of Labour from the trade union whose members were adversely affected.
Supposing there is no trade union?
Any individual may make a complaint.
There is always somebody to write an anonymous letter.

Moreover, under the terms of contract, it is required that all fair wages schedules must be conspicuously posted on the premises, and it is therefore difficult for the contractor to avoid payment of the rates specified, as each workman employed can readily see for himself the rate to which he is entitled for the class of work which is being performed. The experience of the Department of Labour is that in individual cases where the proper wage rates are not being paid, word to this effect has generally reached the department either through the inspections made by departmental officers or through complaints from union officials, or from the workmen themselves. Very many of these adjustments made have to do with the proper classification of the work being done by individual employees. In all cases where it is found that workmen are not receiving proper payment for the class of service rendered, there is no hesitation in enforcing payment of the rates provided in the specification, for the full period involved.
In conclusion, I should like to say that when the department is enlarged, as I hope it will be, we shall be able to pay more attention to this phase of the work. However, I would not want to suggest that there has been any negligence on the part of departmental officers with respect to the enforcement of the fair wage clause. Any complaint which comes into the department is attended to without delay.

I realize that it would be impossible to carry on a strict supervision of all contracts let by the government, and I am glad to have the assurance of the minister that when the department is enlarged more will be done than has been done so far. No doubt there is in the files of the department a list of firms which have been notoriously unfair. Under these circumstances I do not think it would be out of the way to strike off the list of firms allowed to tender on government contracts those concerns known to be unfair, no matter what political stripe they might be. Perhaps the government could make up a sort of blacklist. In the past, blacklists of employees have been issued, so perhaps a blacklist of employers could be made up. I think this would have a good effect on employers in general and would tend to make other employers live up to the terms of their contracts.

I know of no case
during the last few years in which any successful complaint has been made as to a violation of the fair wage provision of government contracts. There have been cases where it was contended that there had been a violation of the fair wage clause by subcontractors. I recall vividly the language usedl ini this house by a former Minister of Labour in connection with wages paid on government contracts. The terms of the contracts are as strict as it is possible to make them in our language. However, on the other hand you have the subcontractor. In five cases out of every ten the work is not done by the original contractor. That was the fact in certain cases to -which I could refer. Pipes, radiators and various items of that sort had been in stock at the time the contract was let. I had to investigate several of these matters and as I felt there must be something wrong, I went as far back as that. We then added to the contract the clause which is now in it referring to subcontractors. That did something to cure the evil.
A clerk of works is appointed on all large contracts. The duty of that clerk is to make a report to the Department of Public Works. Since his attention has been directed to this matter, this clerk now reports, first, that a notice has been placed in a proper place upon the premises. Them he reports as to whether or not any complaints have been made and

as to whether or not the going wages as provided by the Department of Labour are actually being paid to the workmen. His job is to watch the progress of the undertaking. But we have not got past the subcontractor phase in its entirety. I cannot agree with my hon. friend in his suggestion as to blacklists. The very use of that word recalls memories of speeches in this house about the evils of blacklists; it was contended that these were almost as bad as the black plague or the black death.
