Mr. Chairman, I have in mind a different sort of contractor from the one referred to by the leader of the opposition. In connection with many of these contracts there will be subcontractors doing some excavating work. It is men like these who are usually the culprits. They hire people who are more or less connected with or dependent upon them, particularly in times of unemployment. They pay very small wages and no one knows anything about it. I remember several years ago we had a fair wage clause in the contracts let by the city of Regina for the erection of an additional building at the general hospital, and it was thought that fair wages were being paid. Not until some time afterwards did we discover that there was something which seemed to be collusion, and as a matter of fact the men who had been employed at lower than the fair wage were able to collect substantial sums. That is the type of subcontractor whom it is very difficult to deal with; yet he is the one who is something like a parasite upon labour. I thought it well to bring this to the attention of the department so that it might be guarded against so far as possible, although I know it is a very difficult matter to deal with.

There is another situation which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I had a memorandum sent to me only this morning in regard to the condition on the waterfront in Vancouver. It seems that until a short time ago the freight handling, carloading, on the government owned Ballantyne pier and Lapointe pier was done by a certain group of longshoremen at the rate of 60 cents per hour straight time, that is from eight a.m. to five

p.m., and 90 cents per hour overtime, which is any time outside those hours and all day Sunday. Now the rate is 50 cents per hour for any hour of the day or night, and the overtime rate applies on Sunday only.
The suggestion is that these rates have been altered by the Shipping Federation of British Columbia. The shipping federation is said to consist of certain dock operators and stevedoring companies and agents or representatives of various shipping lines, mostly foreign lines, together with harbour officials of the Dominion of Canada. It seems that these harbour officials sit in with this board. I do not know their exact relationship to the board, but the wages are determined by the shipping federation. This board refuses to recognize the I.L.A., the International Longshoremen's Association, as the name suggests, an international union. The question arises, what chance, under those conditions, have thesse men of having any voice in the fixing of their wages?
The men in their memorandum refer to what they state is order in council 7143, dated July 11, 1918. I have not checked this up, but I assume it is correct. Order in council No. 7143 provides that all employees have the right to organize in trades unions; that this right shall not be denied or interfered with in any manner whatsoever, and that through their chosen representatives the employees shall be permitted and encouraged* to negotiate with employers concerning working conditions, rates of pay and other grievances.
Now these men have organized, but the shipping federation refuses to recognize them; it will not deal with them, and consequently they have no voice whatsoever. The men say. Why should the dominion government not carry out the spirit of this order in council and insist upon the recognition of the union, more particularly when the dominion government, through its representatives, sits in with the shipping federation which determines the rate of wages?
There is one other point which they bring up. They refer to what they say is the fact that during the waterfront trouble in Vancouver in 1935:
A delegation of longshoremen were told on Tune 13, 1935, by a committee of the Shipping Federation of British Columbia that the Shipping Federation of British Columbia intended to smash all unions in British Columbia ports, take control of all waterfront work in British Columbia, and after that to give their fullest cooperation to the Pacific Coast Waterfront Employers in a campaign to crack open all unions down the Pacific coast. That proves the international interests of this body, in which the Canadian government is an acquiescing partner.

It does seem to me that the government has a distinct responsibility in a matter of this kind. This may possibly be a matter which comes under the new transport department, but at the same time the conditions are directly related to the work of the labour department. I wish we could have a statement from the minister in regard to the policy of the government.
I take it that this memorandum relates back to a situation which developed on the Vancouver waterfront some time ago.
That condition prevails to-day.
Quite, but as a result of the situation which developed more than a year ago. As a matter of fact, a commissioner, Mr. Justice Davis of the supreme court dealt with the dispute then in existence.
Between the international and the other union.

Between the international and the shipping federation. As a result in large measure of his report, peace eventually was restored upon the Vancouver waterfront. My hon. friend will no doubt suggest that peace was restored, but not upon a satisfactory basis. As I understand it, the present position is this. The shipping federation of Vancouver has entered into an agreement extending over a period of years with two other longshoremen's organizations in Vancouver, and the bulk of the membership of these two organizations which now have an agreement with the shipping federation were formerly within the membership of the International Longshoremen's Association. The International Longshoremen's Association at present contains a smaller number of members than the two organizations which made this agreement with the shipping federation.
The right of association clearly does not carry with it any compulsion upon an employer to adopt the principle of the closed shop. There is a clear distinction between the two things. The right of association does mean and ought to mean that no employer should be guilty of discrimination; in other words, no employer should deprive any employee of his employment because he has been active in the organization of a union. But that does not carry with it the recognition of a particular labour organization as the exclusive organization with which a particular employer should enter into an agreement.

Before the dinner recess the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) asked whether I would place before the committee the letter from Empire Cotton Mills, Limited, in which that company declined to consent to the setting up of a board of conciliation. I have the letter before me. It is rather long, but I doubt whether it would suit the full purpose of my hon. friend if I did not place the entire letter on Hansard. It is addressed to the Deputy Minister of Labour, who is also registrar under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. The letter reads:
February 4, 1937.
Dear Sir:
We beg to acknowledge your letter of the 28th ultimo referring to an application on behalf of the textile workers formerly employed in our Welland plant for the establishment of a board of conciliation and investigation under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.
Although it seems clear that the act, a copy of which you enclosed, does not provide for such a case as the present strike at Welland, where some of our former employees struck without notice, and without any intimation of any desire to discuss any alleged grievances,
and although the present application has not been made until after thirty days from the commencement of the strike, so that none of the strikers are employees within the meaning of the statute, we have, nevertheless, given very careful and sympathetic attention to your request that we should give the application favourable consideration.
We should add that you will observe the applicants have been unable to complete the required statutory declaration which is a condition precedent to the valid establishment of a board, because, of course, they have been unable truthfully to declare that "a strike will be declared."
If we are right in our conclusion that there is no statutory authority in the present circumstances to appoint a board, any board which you might appoint would lack what authority would be conferred upon it if it could be validly appointed under the statute, and further than this, it would have no authority to inquire into many other circumstances related to this strike, amongst which we may mention the circumstances under which a United States union now under suspension by the American Federation of Labour, has attempted by methods of intimidation, the use of the administration of public relief funds, and illegal violence, to induce many of our former employees to join that union.
This union was not present at the commencement of this strike, but has apparently seized upon the opportunity presented to further its own objectives. Whilst doing this it ignores the true facts of the situation and for its own ends, through promises of impossible rates of pay, uses the workers to their own detriment as well as to the general detriment of the community, thereby demonstrating this union's incapability of assuming any of the responsibilities usually undertaken by such bodies. These circumstances have been important contributing factors to the continuation of the strike, and while we would welcome investigation by competent authority we have come to the conclusion that it would be inadvisable to concur in the appointment of a board which would, in fact, have no statutory authority.
We will, however, be glad to cooperate with your department in any efforts which may seem to afford any chance of bringing the unfortunate situation in Welland to a close, and therefore we would welcome any opportunity to discuss the matter further with you.
We have already written to your chief conciliation officer on the 15th January outlining our views in connection with the strike and we wish to emphasize:
First: That we have already restored approximately the 1929 wage scale or better before the strike was commenced. That our policy is to pay the wage rates prevailing in the textile industry in Canada for the same class of work and efficiency under similar conditions, but in many instances we pay higher than the current rates.
Second: That while we have every desire to keep the mill operating, we can afford to go no farther under present conditions. We have already filed returns and given your department information as to this and will be glad to furnish any further particulars you may require.
Third: That -while there has been some talk of grievances with regard to mill conditions,

Supply-Labour-Fair Wages
etc., you will see that the enclosed draft agreement sent to the company under date of 9th January, 1937, apparently dealing with the demands of those directing the strike, provides for an increase of wages, but makes no reference to any other grievances with regard to conditions except for the general provision for discussion of such grievances as might arise. As we have already granted the greatest amount of increase which we can afford, we regret that we cannot suggest a compromise on wages. We always welcome, however, constructive suggestions for improvement of working conditions, and apply all reasonable remedies found to be within the means of the company, but this does not appear to be a real factor in the present strike.
Several of the former employees who desired to go on working, and desired to confer with us with regard to the strike, have been physically prevented by illegal methods of mass-picketing and violence from conferring with our officers. On one occasion, the mass-pickets on the public streets seized and turned the motor cars in which some of our former employees were endeavouring to come to the mill for a conference with our officers. On other occasions our office employees have been assaulted, traffic, including shipments of goods in and out of our premises was interfered with and for a time prevented by violence in the public streets.
While we deplore the continuance of the strike and the resulting unemployment of many of our former workers who desire to work, including those who have been misled by outsiders, we find that it is simply impossible for us to make further increases under present conditions other than those which have already been made.
We are, and have always been ready to meet our employees and discuss grievances with them, but we cannot think that it would serve any useful purpose to have a board of conciliation and investigation established without statutory authority on the request of an affiliate of a foreign union which has, at least, joined in conducting this strike by illegal methods.
The letter is signed by F. L. Mitchell on behalf of Empire Cotton Mills, Limited. He signs as assistant to the president.
What is meant by a foreign union?
Perhaps I ought not to try to explain what was in the mind of the person who wrote the letter. I would assume that he would be referring to a union which has its head office in the United States.
Or other foreign country.
Or other foreign country.

To anyone who has not listened to or read some of the evidence which came out before the Turgeon commission, it is really touching to note this company's concern for the welfare of the employees, and the way in which they are being exploited by these foreign agitators. It is really very touching to anyone who does not know the circumstances, but it seems to

me that their refusal, at any rate as far as the letter which the minister has read is concerned, is very weak. What statutory authority could a board of conciliation have? If the company were willing to have a board appointed, the board could hear evidence and investigate any matter which they might be asked to look into. I have taken part in the proceedings of many boards of conciliation and am quite well aware that their findings are not binding on either side, but I also know that the side which refuses to present its case has not a very good case with the public. Speaking broadly, I believe it is seldom that one side or the other refuses to accept the award of a conciliation board, because generally when they do they lose the public sympathy that they might otherwise have. So there are few awards turned down, even if they are considered by one side to be unsatisfactory, as is bound to happen in any case.

The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) also asked if I could make a more extensive statement as to the matter at issue in this dispute. I have looked up the file and I find it contains the wage rates now applicable in Welland.
I wonder whether they should be placed on Hansard.

I doubt whether it would serve any useful purpose. They cover the entire field of operations. They are provided confidentially to the department, as they are to the bureau of statistics, from time to time. They cover many pages. Perhaps I might repeat what is, after all, the essential matter at issue, namely, that the employees had asked for an increase of twenty per cent in the existing wage rates; the company declared that it had already granted an increase of six per cent, that the wage rates had been restored to the 1929 level, and that the operations of the company in Welland did not permit it to grant the increases demanded by the employees.
I should like to ask the minister a question under item 179, limitation of hours of work.
That is a later item.
Certain articles appeared in the press to the effect that married men were receiving only $9 per week in the Welland mill. I should like to know if those were full-time or part-time employees.

The information we have
does not make a distinction between married

Supply-Labour-Fair Wages
and unmarried employees. I doubt whether we have the information which would enable
me to confirm or dispute that statement.

I asked whether these were
full-time or part-time employees.

That information does not appear to be on our files. Generally speaking, the low paid employees in textile operations are women, and the wages of women are governed by the Minimum Wage Act in Ontario.

My information is that the
notices which appeared in the press to the effect that married' men were receiving only 89 per week were perhaps erroneous in this way, that they were only part-time employees, not full-time.
I am sorry I have not that information before me. It is material, certainly; I shall be glad to secure further information on that point.

It seems to me that the document read to us a few minutes ago is so drawn as to prejudice people generally against the claims of the workers. For instance, as regards this foreign union business, the fact is that nearly all1 the unions in this country have their headquarters in the United States, the international unions. We have had Tom Moore here a considerable time and in this house again and again he has been lauded. He presided until recently over the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, which may almost be said to be the Canadian section of the American Federation of Labour. It is ridiculous that we should have these held up as foreign unions, and then, as soon as a Canadian union starts up, be told that it must be disregarded because "we want to deal with the well-established, recognized, international unions." Further, we are told that these organizers came in later. What can the men do but bring in the organizer of the union with which they wish to unite? We were told this afternoon that in a great many concerns the wage scales are posted in the plant. Is that true in this case?

If I might correct my
hon. friend, the reference was to fair wage scales applicable to public works and work done under contract with the government.

I am glad to have the correction. It seems to me that in a matter of this kind where there has been no union recognized, where apparently the company refuses to recognize the union, it is very difficult indeed for the employees to know what is the prevailing wage. They know
what they are paid, but they do not know what is the general wage. Whatever may be the ethics of the department in not giving this information, to the public. I would say that, especially where there is no union, it is of interest to the public to know what wages are being paid in these factories. It is absurd for us to spend time in parliament discussing this case if all we know is that there has been a gain of six per cent. We do not know what it means; we do not know what the wage was before that increase. All we hear now is that this company adheres to the prevailing rates. Well, if the rates prevailing in Welland are those which prevailed in the factories which the Turgeon commission has been investigating, it is a disgrace to this country that any such institution should be allowed to keep its doors open. I think the responsibility is on the Department of Labour tc make an investigation in this particular case and let the public know the facts. That is the only way the employees have any chance of defence unless they take the law into their own hands.

I hope my hon. friend will acquit me of any intention of placing upon Hansard information which is prejudicial to the employees in this case. He will1 recall that I placed this letter upon Hansard at the request of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis).
No; I am speaking of the tone of the letter and the form: in which some of the statements are made.

It occurs to me that not only may the minister be warranted in doing it, but it is his duty to indicate the rate per hour being paid to workmen in that factory. It is obvious that if there were a public inquiry those wages would be made known. In the Turgeon investigation wages were always made public. I cannot think that a letter sent to the minister or the department indicating the wages paid can be regarded as a confidential communication. On the other hand, I would not suggest that the minister should undertake to place on Hansard all that vast mass of material, but he should be able to indicate what those working on the looms receive per hour and the number of hours they work per day. He should be able to indicate what other classes of workmen receive for instance, spinners, and those having to do with other branches of activity in the manufacture of the product. I think there is force in what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) says when he suggests that we are discussing a matter about which unfortunately our knowledge is

Supply-Labour-Fair Wages
limited. I suggest to the minister that it is no violation of any possible confidence if he makes known to the committee and the country the rate of wages per hour being paid to the various classes of employees, both men and women, and I believe this could be done without much difficulty. I should think it would not take more than half a column in Hansard, because the divisions of labour are not very numerous, unless it is a mill that makes many products.

I assure the committee that I have no desire at all to withhold this information, but in the form in which it has been presented I doubt whether it would be intelligible. The schedules cover a great many different piece-work operations. Perhaps this is a confession of ignorance upon my part, but I am bound to say that it does not convey to me the information which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre desires to have. I shall be glad to see if it is not possible to put it into the form suggested by the leader of the opposition.
That should be possible.
I shall be glad to see if that cannot be done.
The several divisions are not numerous and the rates per hour can be ascertained.

If we are going to get any information of that sort, I would suggest that the last suggestion be looked into, that of giving the hours of work. After all, a moment ago the minister mentioned piecework in these factories, and we know that in some factories men are not able to work the maximum number of hours per day or per week. Consequently a wage of $9 a week for part-time work is not uncommon. But that part-time work is really all the work these men can do on account of the operations they perform. I think in dealing with social security legislation and labour conditions, we shall have to take that factor in industry into account. I know that in a large plant of which I had some knowledge several years ago, men would go out and stand around for four or five hours a day waiting for work which would last three or four or five hours. While the rate probably looked all right, the aggregate amount of money that one of those men could earn in a week was relatively small.
I think a community is interested in the matter from this point of view: If men are unable to make enough money in their ordinary avocation to maintain themselves and their families, then when times become bad

they become charges upon the community, and the community really has to bear part of the cost of industry, which I think should be borne by industry itself. If this matter of wages and hours could be looked into and reported upon, that side of the question might also be investigated.

I should like to say just one further word on this point. I am informed by the officers of the department that this particular information is given to the department confidentially. I mention that for this reason, that so far as I am aware there is no law which compels these companies to provide this information, inasmuch as it may affect their competitive position in relation to other companies operating within the same fields. I would think that at all events it would be desirable to look into that aspect of the question. I simply state that as a reservation upon what I said just a moment ago. For my part I have no objection whatever to bringing this information before the committee provided it can be done without prejudice to the position of the Department of Labour in relation to these firms that are reporting to us for statistical purposes.

Could the item
stand, then, until we hear the decision of the minister?

Perhaps the point could be discussed upon some other appropriate item, with the clear understanding that meanwhile I shall look into the point raised by my hon. friend. I can assure him that I shall obtain the information without delay and present the reasons for or against the policy which has been followed in the past.

If the information is
received as confidential, it must be treated as such, but I suggest that it cannot possibly be treated in that way, notwithstanding what the officials say, for the simple and obvious reason that at the recent inquiry the evidence was forthcoming as to what was paid in every factory in Canada.
An investigation by a royal commission.

By a royal commission,,
of course, but a royal commission is the creature of this parliament, by a statute, it is true. But let me put this to the minister:	This cannot possibly affect the competitive position of anyone, for the very letter which was read indicates that they were paying the going rate, that it was the 1929 rate, and further it is alleged that it is an even higher wage than is warranted by the scale in the locality. I wholly agree that the min-

ister must assume a position which will protect the information that has been given to a minister of the crown or to a department as confidential, and that confidence can be removed only by the people who, relying upon it, furnished the information. But I submit that this cannot be so regarded. What is sought is not what the officials are talking about. It is the rate per hour and the number of hours per day that men work. I would undertake to get that information in half an hour in Welland to-night. This story about not being able to understand something -why, it is the duty of these officials to clear it up so that the minister can understand it. It seems to me absurd that in the twentieth century a minister has to rise in his place in the house and say he cannot understand what these figures mean as to the wages paid in industry. How much do they pay per hour to men and women; what are the classifications, and how many hours per day do they work? It seems to me that information should not be difficult to obtain. I am sure if the minister and I went to Welland to-night we would have that information before bedtime without any trouble at all. There is nothing of secrecy or anything like that about it; it is a plain, simple story as to what people are getting per hour and per day, and the number of hours they work per day.

My statement, as I think
the leader of the opposition fully acknowledges, was made in recognition of the position which a minister must maintain with respect to information which is given to him confidentially.

What is so confidential
about it?

My right hon. friend has
referred to the fact that the royal commission on textiles has secured this type of information. That is quite true, but a royal commission has full powers under the Inquiries Act to take evidence of this kind under oath. In other words, the information may be said to be extracted even from an unwilling witness. On the other hand, I am informed that this information was presented to the department confidentially, and that is the only reservation I make. I would have no desire at all to withhold anything from the committee or the house.

Then, would the
minister secure the information from the employees, who would be quite willing to give it? Would it be possible for the department to secure a statement from the employees as to what they were paid?
I can only say that I shall secure it in the best possible way with the least possible delay.

In securing this information I hope the minister will bear in mind the peculiar manner in which a good part of the help employed in the cotton industry is paid; that is, by the piece, and also the fact that if these men worked a certain number of hours for a certain number of days they might earn so much. But from my experience, after many hours of labour in a cotton mill, it is difficult to gauge what the weekly wage is going to be, for a weaver in particular.
Exactly. In other words the schedules do not mean a great deal.

They do not mean a great deal. For instance, if a mill is rushed, they will see that the weaver is amply supplied with the wherewithal to continue operating, but I know that in cotton mills where there is not a tremendous amount of work on hand, work is backed up either in the slashing room or in the spinning room, and for that reason a weaver is unemployed for a certain period of time during ithe day. He is there, but probably he is running only fifty per cent of his looms, or even fewer than that.
Then we must also bear in mind this fact, which I have always felt was unjust to the labourer: He will weave his piece, which will be taken to the cloth room. There it is examined and flaws are discovered. These flaws may be the fault of the weaver or they may be the fault of anything else connected with the development of that piece, but he is called up and fined for these errors or omissions or mistakes. There again the wage of the man is affected. The fine might be only twenty-five cents or it might run as high as two or three dollars. That has a very definite bearing. So, if these figures are to be secured, in justice to the men I feel some reference should be had to the conditions under which they work. I do not want figures placed on the table showing that a weaver running six or eight looms is getting $15 per week, when that figure would represent only what he could earn if he were running those six looms for six days a week, eight hours a day.
Some one has already pointed out that probably his wage for the week is only $8 or $9. Personally I believe that through the Department of Labour some adjustment in the wages of these people should be made. They can be dealt with most unfairly, and can be made pay the cost of slack time, although being actually within the mill for the full length of time during any one week. The minister ought to

bear that in mind when he is getting the information, and make absolutely certain that we are getting correctt information and not that which is liable to be misleading. Probably if he got it from the employer and also from the employee, and struck an average, he might get a figure which would be nearer the truth than if he were to obtain the information from only one source. Then, again, I would not place too much confidence in any report which might be developed through the recent inquiry, which is more or less a political window-dressing-the Turgeon inquiry into the textile industry.

When the committee took recess, the minister was answering some questions asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) concerning the situation on the Vancouver waterfront. Has he that information now?

I take it the particular point in the mind of the hon. member is that the harbour commission was represented in the shipping federation, which entered into the agreements of which he makes complaint. I believe he is correct in his belief that the representatives of the harbour commission in the past have sat in with the shipping federation with respect to the determination of wage agreements with longshoremen.

But since the harbour
commission went out, what? What has happened since it ceased to exist? There is no longer a harbour commission.
No; but there is a port manager, and the harbour commission still functions as such in the city of Vancouver. Perhaps the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) could give us information on that point.

The previous local harbour board was a member of the shipping federation. Since the central board came into being, consideration has been given the matter, and my view is that we should not be members of the federation. We are large employers of waterfront labour. Just at the time we were dissociating ourselves from the federation, the labour trouble came on and made it inadvisable to change the position at that time. However, I believe I can say that within the next few months we shall dissociate ourselves from the federation.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gave briefly the information he had received from the International Longshoremen's Association in Vancouver. As

I understand it-and I had some contact with the organization last summer-the situation is this: In 1923 there was a strike on the waterfront between the International Longshoremen's Association and the employers. The longshoremen lost that strike and from then until 1933 there was no workers' organization on the waterfront. In 1933 another organization known as the Coastwise Longshore and Freight Handlers Association was formed. Then, in 1935, there was another strike. In the fall of 1935 a local of the International Longshoremen's Association was organized but was not recognized by the shipping federation. The unions that were recognized by the shipping federation were the strikebreakers who had been taken in during the strike. Nevertheless men connected with the International Longshoremen's Association were doing some work on the waterfront, particularly for the Kingsley Navigation Company Limited.
Coastwise shipping?

I am not sure, but I
believe they had deep-sea vessels; at least I was so informed.
How much were they being paid?

I cannot say what they were paid, but I shall show later that the pay as well as the work was satisfactory. On October 1 of this year the International Longshoremen's Association was informed by the Kingsley Navigation Company Limited that they would not continue to employ association members, because that company was a member of the shipping federation, and the federation insisted that they do not employ members of the association. The minister stated before recess that recognition of a union did not necessarily mean recognition of a closed shop, but I suggest that in this instance it does mean a closed shop. It means a shop in which certain workers belonging to certain unions cannot obtain work.
But does it not follow, when a company enters into an agreement with a particular union, that employment shall be given to the members of that union?

Yes, but the union had an agreement with the Kingsley Navigation Company. However, this company was a member of the shipping federation and this federation, which controlled all shipping on the coast, insisted that only members of their union should be employed. The complaint of the longshoremen is that officials of the Vancouver harbour board sit in with the shipping federation and agree to this unjust

Supply-Labour-Fair Wages
discrimination. I hope the Minister of Transport will find ways and means of overcoming the difficulty, and the federal government will not be associated' with a condition of this kind.

Prior to the recess the Minister of Labour said: he would try to find out something about the Empire Cotton Mills, Limited, of Welland. He said he would try to learn whether they are part of another corporation, and, if not who the officers of the organization may be.

I had not forgotten the question. During the recess I was informed that the Empire Cotton Mills, Limited, was associated with the Woods Manufacturing Company, with head office at Hull. I have not been able to determine precisely the nature of the relationship between them.
Does not the government give fairly substantial contracts to the Woods company?
I am not able to answer that question.

I am under the impression that the Woods company of Hull at different times have been the recipient of government contracts. If such is the case, I believe there is ample opportunity for the government to bring pressure to bear.

He is now.

A few minutes ago the leader of the opposition asked the number of disputes and the minister said seven. I turn up the auditor general's report and I find there were eight. The minister now tells me that these eight were in the previous year. I should like to see this bookkeeping speeded up so that we shall have before us the particulars of what we want to discuss.
The Labour Gazette, which is published monthly, gives that information from time to time. It will also be found in the report of the Department of Labour which is tabled each year.

The minister said there

That ought to be a good argument for conciliation in labour disputes.

What does this item cover?

This appropriation is intended to cover expenses for printing, stationery and other supplies, travelling expenses, and so forth in the administration of the Employment Offices Coordination Act. The amount of $9,000 submitted for the fiscal year 1937-38 is $750 less than was voted for the current year, leaving for the supplementary estimates any deficit arising out of the reorganization.
There is another item in the estimates of the department providing for a statutory contribution under the Employment Offices Coordination Act.
How many of these offices are there now in Canada?
There are sixty-six throughout the dominion.
Do our Canadian employment offices carry on the same work as the employment offices in Great Britain?

I would not go so far as to say that the service of the employment offices in Canada has yet reached a state of usefulness equal to that of the labour exchanges in Great Britain. The present situation is not wholly satisfactory. The dominion government makes an annual contribution to the provinces, and the aotual employment offices are maintained by the provinces, which select the site and determine the personnel. The dominion office exists largely for the purpose of coordinating the work of these offices and compiling information on a national scale. My feeling is that much still requires to be done in order that the employment service in Canada may do the work that it can usefully do.

At the moment there is a boom or the prospect of a boom in steel foundries throughout the country. A few days ago I was talking to a foundryman who told me that he had increased his staff to about two thousand men, and would be taking on more. I wondered at the time whether the Canadian employment service, either federal or provincial-apparently from what the minister says the federal office does not do much along the line of employment-assists, like the employment offices in Great Britain, in transferring steel workers, for instance, who may be out of work in Welland to, say Sault Ste. Marie, or steel workers out of work in Owen
Sound back to Hamilton. Do our employment agencies do anything along the line of transferring men from one part of the country to another as they do in England?

Yes. I think it might be useful if I gave the following information.
During the fiscal year 1935-36 the offices of the employment service of Canada registered for employment a total of 677,408 applicants, men and women; listed 375,169 opportunities for work, notified by employers; placed in work 351,886 applicants.
In 7.787 cases of placement, applicants were assisted to move to employment by a special reduced transportation rate of 2-7 cents per mile given by the railways for use by the employment offices, where persons being placed are travelling to employment at a distance where the fare is more than $4.
Of the total of 353,802 placements made, 114,731 were non-local, that is, were made in municipalities other than those in which the placing offices are located.

I agree with the statement of the minister that the operation of these offices is quite unsatisfactory. Is it not true that the employment council of Canada acts in an advisory capacity to the minister? Did the council meet in the last calendar year, and were recommendations made to which the assent of the provincial governments might be desired?

I am informed that the National Employment Service Council met early in 1930, or at any rate at some period in 1930, and has not been convened since. I would point out that to some extent the functions which would be performed by the council have been transferred for the time being to the National Employment Commission. I am far from saying that the composition of the National Employment Service Council was not such as would make it a really useful body, particularly at a period when there was expanding employment. I assume it was not summoned in the last six years because it was felt that there was not sufficient opportunity for it to render service.
Who is responsible for the staff of the labour bureaux throughout Canada?
The staff of the bureaux is selected entirely by the provincial governments.

How many offices are in operation in British Columbia?
Supply-Labour
Eight: at Kamloops, Nanaimo, Nelson, New Westminster, Penticton, Prince Rupert. Vancouver, Victoria.
What are the functions of these offices with respect to the registration of transient unemployed?

No duties with respect to
the registration of transient unemployed are imposed upon these officers by the federal government. It is possible they have been utilized by provincial governments for that purpose, but we would not necessarily have knowledge of that fact.

The minister indicated that
approximately half of the requests for work are filled by employment offices throughout the country. Has he a classification of the type of work that was found for these people?

I have not that information before me. I am not certain at the moment whether it is obtainable at once in the form suggested by my hon. friend. I take it he would wish to know how many have been transferred to woods operations, how many to relief work, how many to factory work-
And farm placement.

As far as farm placement
is concerned, under the existing scheme with the province that information is available, but I suppose my hon. friend is interested in farm placement apart from any scheme of government assistance.

Is there no farm placement
within this category?

I have before me for the
previous year a report printed by the Department of Labour. The hon. member would have no difficulty in securing a copy of it. I could read or place it on Hansard, but I shall be glad to see that he receives a copy of it.

Does not the Department of Labour assume responsibility for the policy of placement in Canada? I have reference to the policy as applied to single, unemployed women transients and the difficulties they encounter in being placed in domestic service. Does not the federal government assure these women suitable protection when migrating from one province to another for placement in domestic service? Does the government see that they are protected against unscrup-pulous employers? It has been brought to my attention recently that there have been sent to questionable sections of cities a number of young women in destitute circumstances whose situation has been taken advantage of by the touts of the underworld.

Cannot the federal government exercise supervision to ensure that when any young woman seeks employment and is sent to some address she shall be given reasonable protection and be placed with respectable people?

On that point, we do not
interfere directly in the administration of employment offices within the provinces. We have assumed, rightly I believe, that the provincial officers who have special responsibility in this matter would! have the same desire that our own officers would have to prevent the sort of abuses described by my hon. friend. If, on the other hand, he has any complaint or if we receive complaints that these abuses do occur, we shall certainly be pleased to take them up with the provincial governments concerned, The general administration has, however, been left to them.
What is the total cost to the federal government of the operation of these offices?

That comes under another item in the labour estimates, authorized by statute-the organization and coordination of employment offices, under the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. The cost is $150,000 a year.
Is that all it costs the federal government?

That is the total federal
contribution.

What is the total cost of
running these offices throughout the dominion?

Perhaps I might put on

Returning to the question of single unemployed women, I have no complaint against the officials in charge of the various offices, but the impression seems to be that they lack adequate facilities to deal with this very serious matter, and I was wondering whether the minister would not consider some extension of this service so that

Supply-Labour
a more satisfactory placement might be accomplished and proper protection afforded young women in the circumstances to which I have referred.

I shall be glad to look
into the question raised by my hon. friend with a view to removing any abuses that do exist.

To what extent are these
various offices in Canada attempting to reclassify the unemployed? I understand that many are now engaged in a reclassification to determine those who are actually unemployable.

The employment commission has been proceeding with a re-registration and classification of the unemployed on relief, and some provinces may be supplementing that by an attempt to reclassify the unemployed whether they are on relief or not. We had a discussion on this point last year. It does not seem feasible to take a general census of the unemployed. Indeed, it is doubtful whether such a census could be taken accurately without taking a complete census of Canada. That has been the experience of the United States. It was thought at one time that they could take a census of the unemployed separately, but I believe the conclusion has been reached that they could not obtain accurate results in that way. I agree that the employment offices might serve a useful purpose in the direction suggested by my hon. friend, and certainly, with employment opportunities improving, it is all the more important that there should be a more precise classification of all those who register at employment offices.

If, in the reclassification
now actually under way, a person in receipt of relief is listed as unemployable, what steps are taken to determine responsibility for further payment of relief to that individual?

At the present time those who are listed as unemployable are so listed by the municipalities, and I think we are justified in taking it for granted that the test of unemployability is almost entirely a health test. That is, I do not believe that what might be termed occupational disabilities are taken into consideration. I mean by that phrase not disabilities attaching to the occupation, but rather the loss of power to practise an occupation owing to long years of idleness. I do not think one can say that our present test of unemployability is wholly satisfactory. There is a strong pressure on municipalities to narrow the definition, for the reason that it has generally been accepted that care for the unemployable is primarily their responsibility; therefore the tendency is for municipalities to put a rather narrow construction upon that term, and to confine it to those who are completely incapable of performing physical labour.
Who then accepts responsibility for their relief?

In most of the provinces unemployables have simply gone on the relief rolls. That is one question we have to face in this country, namely, that our relief rolls do not consist solely of unemployed who have become unemployed as a result of the depression. That is one element, and we can still say the predominant element, but our relief rolls also contain those who formerly received poor law assistance in some provinces and municipalities and those who might be termed charitable cases. In fact, where formerly we had a number of distinct classifications, those classifications have now tended to disappear; the boundaries, such as they were, between them have been blurred in consequence. It is going to be a problem of great difficulty and magnitude to restore that distinction between unemployment due to physical disability and unemployment due to lack of opportunity for work.
Where would the minister draw the line between the two?

I would prefer not to be drawn into a statement on that point at this time. I think that discussion would be more appropriate when the special supplementary estimates are before the house. I have no desire to curtail discussion on the point, for it is most interesting, but there will be full opportunity to bring it up at that time.
Would the minister say there are more unemployables to-day than there were prior to the depression; that the depression has caused many to become unemployable?
I would agree that it is probably so, but I do not know of anyone who can state accurately the extent to which long idleness tends to create unemployability.

If the distinction is reestablished between those who are unemployed and those who are unemployable, and that distinction is made in order to place upon the local authorities the responsibility which they formerly had, then, if that is the purpose of making the distinction, I submit that is an almost impossible burden in view of the financial condition of the municipalities.

I was careful to avoid saying that was necessarily the purpose.

I noticed the minister was careful to avoid making that statement, but I wondered whether that had been considered, because I think it is impossible for the municipalities to bear the cost of those who have become unemployable as a result of the depression.
