speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: It might be useful, with the indulgence of the committee, if I made a brief statement concerning the reorganization of several departments into the Department of Mines and Resources. Hon, members will recall that the legislation necessary to effect this reorganization was passed last session. That legislation provided for the possible setting-up of eight directorships. A committee consisting of the proposed deputy minister of the department and several of the other senior officials spent about two months in working out the details of the reorganization. It finally resulted in the setting-up of five branches in the new department. Those branches consist of the Mines and Geology branch, the Lands, Parks and Forests branch, the Surveys and Engineering branch, the Indian Affaire branch, and the Immigration branch. In addition, there was set up under the immediate direction of the deputy minister the Administrative services branch, which supervises the work of all branches in relation to personnel. The purchasing of all departments is centralized in this office, also the legal section, the editorial and publicity section and the mail distributing section. It will be recalled that this new department is a combination of four former departments, namely the Department of Mines, the Department of Immigration, the Department of the Interior and the Department of Indian Affairs. As hon. members will recall, most of those departments had editorial sections, publicity branches and engineering services.
They did not have in 1935.
Well, I think they had.
No.
About $8 a head.
Yes, almost $9 a head. Medical services and hospitalization for the same period required $940,000, and the amount spent on education was $1,936,000.
That is the largest item.

Yes, that is the largest item. For the current year which will end on March 31 next, I am afraid our relief costs and our costs for medical care and hospitalization will be even larger than they were in the previous year. This is due to the fact, as far as relief is concerned, that the manner of living of the Indians has changed as compared with the way they lived in years gone by. For instance, in the northern part of the prairie provinces, and to a great extent in British Columbia, the Indians lived mainly by trapping and fishing. I believe I stated to the house a year ago-if not I shall give the information to-night-that twenty-five years ago there was an annua, shipment from the northern part of Manitoba of from 750,000 to 1.000,000 muskrat skins per year. In recent years it has declined to a mere fraction of 1hat number. There are vast areas in Manitoba suitable for no purpose other than the raising of fur-bearing animals. The same holds true of eastern Manitoba.
Last autumn in Winnipeg one of our Indian agents told me that if something were not done to improve trapping conditions in that part of Manitoba, within five years practically all the Indians would be on relief. We spent a small amount last year and, if I can



Supply-Mines and Resources
get the appropriation, will spend some money this year in creating conditions to bring back the fur, particularly in the northern part of Manitoba. It has been demonstrated elsewhere that this can be done. For instance, muskrats are bred in the state of Louisiana to a point where the annual production of muskrat skins approximates about 6,000,000. The pelts are much inferior to those produced in Canada, and if we go about the business in a proper manner I can see no reason why fur cannot be brought back in Canada, as it has been elsewhere. Indeed, practical experiments conducted on a small scale have proven beyond question that it can be done.
The great difficulty, so far as the Indian is concerned, has been the invasion by white trappers. The white trapper traps clean. It will be of interest to hon. members to know that in the winter of 1936-36 a trapper in the northwest territories used an aeroplane to look after his trap lines. He had qualified for a pilot's licence, had bought a plane, and his trap lines stretched over about 125 miles, following a series of waterways and lakes. The effect was to drive the Indians from that trapping area. We are regulating the trapping by aeroplane because we have learned there are other trappers qualifying to get pilots' licences, and it would have been only a short time until a considerable amount of relief would have been required in this part of the northwest territories. I am already discussing with one or two of the provinces the possibility of setting aside areas adjacent to Indian reserves at which points the trapping will be confined exclusively to Indians. Those negotiations are not yet to a point where I can give further information to the committee. I feel, however, that this aspect of the Indian problem is one of considerable gravity.
I am hopeful, too, that we may be able to make some improvements in our educational endeavours among the Indians. May I bear willing tribute to the splendid work done by the Christian churches of Canada in their effort to raise the standard of living among the Indians. We have seventy-nine residential schools, and in addition a great many day schools. The difficulty in the past in the residential schools was that at perhaps six or seven years of age the Indian boy or girl was taken from the reserve and spent eight or nine years in residential school, where he or she learned about the white man's way of living. When their school terms were over there was nowhere for them to go. other than back to the reserves. This matter is now engaging the serious attention of some of the depart-

mental officials. It is hoped that we may give a training which may be of a more vocational nature than it is at present and thereby make it more valuable to the students. After all, the Indian people in Canada had a culture of a kind. The Indian woman, who perhaps had never seen or been close to white civilization, had developed arts, among which was the art of tanning leather, and making leather goods, some of which were of fine quality.
And bead work.

For instance, we find that
the Indians of Nova Scotia made excellent axe and pick handles, and excellent baskets, but there was no means by which they could market them. We hope to improve that condition, and I feel quite certain it can be done. Far too often when the Indian had acquired a few furs or something he could turn into cash, advantage was taken of his inexperience in marketing and in values. I believe that this offers a useful field for our educational and welfare departments.
Medical costs are very high, and I am not altogether satisfied with the basis upon which our medical services are being carried out. If the Indian has a slight ailment, in too many instances he is taken to the hospital, and -heavy expenses incurred. I make that statement not wishing in the slightest degree to reflect upon the administration. After all, the expenditure is so large that I do believe steps must be taken to try to keep it within bounds, and if possible to reduce it. We have had enough experience to warrant us in the assumption that this can be done. It is a mistake to think the Indian has not intellectual equipment. He has, but it must be directed along the right channel. Above all, our Indian agents and the people entrusted with the administration must have sympathy and understanding, if we are to obtain the best results. I have almost concluded my observations concerning the Indians. Those associated with Indian administration need something -of the missionary spirit and zeal.
The immigration branch is, of course, a stationary one. It may be of interest to hon. members to know that a total of 27,000,000 people were passed last year by immigration authorities. That number, of course, includes people who may have gone back and forth many times across our borders but who, on each occasion, would have to pass the immigration officials. In the fiscal year 1935-36, 11,103 immigrants were admitted to Canada, and in the calendar year 1936, w'hich,

Supply-Mines and Resources
of course, includes part of the figure I have just given, there were 11,643. For the calendar year 1935 there were 11,277. It would appear, therefore, that at the moment immigration to Canada is practically stationary.
I thought lion, members might be interested in this brief review of the organization of the department, and some of the problems in administration we are facing.

When the Minister of Mines brought down his estimates a year ago, he told us that he intended to make a survey of the different branches of the departments under his control, such as mines, Indian affairs and so on. It is encouraging to have the minister state to-night that he has carried out this promise. Personally, I always like to compliment anyone who makes an effort to grasp the matters under his control. It is not my intention at the moment to discuss any branch other than that of mines, particularly iron. During my surveys this summer I came across several places where the minister had been. When the Indian estimates are up later on, I shall have something to say on them. I was very much pleased to hear what he said about the Indians, and I shall be ready to support him in that connection.
In connection with mines, I should like to throw out a suggestion to the minister in connection with a national iron policy. I know the minister was over the Algoma Central last year because I was told he had been there when I made a survey of the Helen iron mine. He may have something along this line in mind. I remember a year ago I said something about the necessity of an iron policy in Canada, and to-day I am more convinced than ever that the time has come when Canada should plan such a policy. A short time ago when there was some talk of trouble in Europe, the great republic to the south passed legislation prohibiting the exportation of war materials to certain European countries. I have been associated with the iron and steel business for some time and I was wondering what would happen in Canada should Great Britain get into some kind of trouble that we could not or should not keep out of and the United States determine that there would have to be a prohibition of the exportation of iron to Canada. Such action would disorganize completely the iron and steel plants in Canada, particularly those which might be engaged in the manufacture of war materials.
As the minister knows, nearly all the iron ore coming into Canada, particularly into Ontario, comes from the Mesaba and other great iron ore regions south of lake Superior. When he was going over the Algoma Central,
31111-43J
the minister undoubtedly heard a good deal about the Helen iron mine and those other great mines up there which are able to produce a low grade ore. The minister may have given considerable thought to this matter, but I should like to see some encouragement given to the development of this so-called low grade ore in Algoma. While I was up there, some engineers and geologists were making a survey as to the possibilities of this ore. I learned that over in Minnesota, where most of the iron ore used in America is produced, outside what is produced in Alabama, they were commencing to use low grade ores. These low grade ores are roasted or sintered in order to take out the carbonate and reduce it to iron _ oxide. I learned that they figure that within reasonable length of time, perhaps twenty-five or fifty years at the outside, the great ranges of Mesabi and those along Iron river and south of lake Superior will become more or less exhausted. In order to protect the great iron and steel industries of the country they are beginning to mix low grade ore with the high grade.
I am informed-the minister and his department heads will know more about this than I do-that with a reasonable expenditure the new Helen mine could be reopened and a commercial product produced by roasting or sintering the ore. If that could be done it would be a great boon to Canada as the iron and steel industry would be safeguarded and the employment of thousands of men protected should the contingency to which I referred before occur.
I went to the top of the Helen mine. This was rather a hard journey for me as it is about 2,800 feet up and it was quite steep in many places. At the top I was able to see the trenches which had been cut across that mountain to reveal the ore. I forget the number of trenches which had been cut, but I was told that there were plainly visible 100,000,000 tons of ore which could be got out quite easily. I went into the mine about 900 feet to the point where they had stopped taking out the ore, I believe in 1918. If the department could plan some economical and reasonable way in which this iron ore could be developed in Algoma, there would be tremendous possibilities for that fine city of Sault Ste. Marie and the other cities in the south which would be able to obtain iron and steel needs from the plant at Sault Ste. Marie. While I had a word or two to say last year about the iron ore industry in Canada, since that time I have covered a lot of territory. I was very much interested to find that in townships of Leeds and Lanark occurred the first iron smelting in Ontario.

Supply-Mines and Resources
Is that hematite ore?
It was a very high grade ore in Leeds when it was taken out.
Is it hematite?

It would be hematite
quality. Hematite means a high grade of iron oxide, and it was high grade ore that was taken out of Leeds. I cannot understand the hon. gentleman as his Scotch is too broad for me, although I am part Scotch myself.

I asked the hon. gentleman
if it was hematite in order to find out whether he knew just what it was.

The Algoma ore that
was taken out of the old Helen mine was hematite, and the ore that is in the New Helen mine is called siderite or iron carbonate.
I know a little bit about the iron business.
I found out that the first iron ore production in Ontario was in the county of Leeds. There was also some production at about the same time in Lanark county, but the larger production occurred in Leeds.
It is very interesting to read what the early administrators of this province had to say about it. About 1784 Major Edward Jessup, a resident, I assume, of either Leeds or Grenville-I used to know a Jessup family in Grenville, in the town of Prescott some years ago, and it may have been one of that family, as they were a military family writing to the governor, said:
As iron is a necessary, expensive and heavy article to transport, and as we are told there is an iron ore bed and a good place to build iron works between the settlements of Oswatia and Catraque, I beg leave to suggest to His Excellency the setting apart of these lands.
That would be for the development of iron ore. It was 1801 before they commenced producing and they produced until 1811. The next start was at Normandale in 1820 on the shores of lake Erie, where for twenty-seven years they produced what is called swamp iron, a very soft iron, almost 100 per cent pure' iron. Then later on production took place at Marmora. All these mines are extinct to-day or, at all events, are not being worked.
The best place to commence, as far as I can see, a national iron ore policy, is the Helen iron mountain in Algoma. Other countries are developing their low grade ores. I read only a few days ago an article stating that the German government had issued orders that all their low grade mines should be put into operation. New methods of roasting the low grade ores make it possible to develop them commercially at not too great a cost. 
The minister, I am sure, has in mind what the former Ontario government did in 1923,
I think it was, to encourage the production of iron in Ontario. The Ferguson government offered to any body of men who would undertake the production of iron ore in Algoma a grant of one cent a unit, about 75 cents per ton for the finished ore. In the state of Minnesota they are mixing a low grade ore to-day with their high grade ore, and if something were done-the government may have already done it, I am speaking from the point of view of one who does not know what is being done-to encourage the development of the New Helen mine, I am sure that that ore could be taken down to Sault Ste. Marie, to be roasted there, and a large tonnage shipped over to Minnesota for mixing with their high grade ore. Of course, the government cannot give a bounty to iron ore that is exported, but such a development would promote the production of a large volume of iron ore for consumption in Canada. We have large steel plants in Hamilton, for example, and I was told in the United States when I was visiting that country last summer that a company over there was entertaining the idea of erecting another steel plant in Canada just as soon as things got a little further advanced. In view of what the government is now doing to assist the railways in spending about $20,000,000 in rehabilitating cars and so forth, the production of iron ore in Canada would help us, if any effort could help us at the moment, by promoting the expenditure of money on every side right from the production of the ore down to the finished product in the cars.
I believe the time is ripe to commence a national iron policy for the production of iron ore in Canada. I was happy to learn recently that the Hepburn government-I cannot very often say anything good about the Hepburn government; perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite can, but they will forgive me for not saying anything particular in its favour-had announced that it would give a grant of one cent a unit for the development of iron ore in Ontario. I am told by engineers that it would be difficult to produce it for a bonus of one cent and that there is little encouragement in one cent a unit, but if the federal government would do what the Ferguson government expected it would do, also vote one cent a unit for the production of iron ore in Ontario, I honestly believe the iron ore business could be started in Canada again, many thousands of men put to work, and great assistance given to the iron foundries in Canada. It would also be of great advantage, in the event of trouble, if the importa-

Supply-Mines and Resources
tion of iron ore into Canada from foreign countries were prohibited. We would then have our own iron for our iron and steel industries, and iron and steel constitute one of the basic industries of the country.
May I ask how much is one cent per unit?

It is the equivalent of 75 cents a ton of the finished ore. That would be approximately $1.50 per ton of finished ore, if both governments contributed. I am not going to get into an argument with my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is very wise.

It is not a case of fearing the hon. gentleman in any way. I have been associated with men working in the iron and steel industry for a long time, and it is difficult for me to argue with someone who knows absolutely less than nothing from the practical standpoint about the production of iron and steel. I would gladly discuss the matter with some practical man who has served in the industry for more than a month or two, and then perhaps we could get somewhere, but economists and all that ilk-save me from them, and save them from me too.
I have finished what I had to say. I rose first to congratulate the minister because I crossed his path on several different occasions this summer, and I was pleased to see that he thought enough of his department to go out through northern Ontario and elsewhere to find out just what could be done about improving his department. I hope that great benefits will result from his trip.
Second, I rose to try to encourage, even in a very humble way-because I have not tried to elaborate on this subject at all as it is hardly up for discussion at the moment- the reopening of what is undoubtedly one of the best low grade iron mines in this country, and the reopening could be done economically I am told, because of the vast improvement in iron roasting machinery. I am told that the New Helen makes really good iron when sintered.
Third, I rose, in the hope that Canada will be placed in the position, in the event of her not being able to obtain ore from outside, of producing her own ore necessities so as to keep her own steel and iron plants in operation in times of trouble, or, better still, in times of peace.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hesitated to interrupt the hon. member in his interesting remarks, but I wish to remind the committee that we are on item 144 for administration of the Explosives Act, and I would suggest-
I followed in the footsteps of the minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would suggest to the committee that if they passed this item, the next two would afford opportunity for a discussion of the subject started by the hon. member.

The discussion was not started by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol). The minister, in introducing his estimates, stated to the committee that he thought it desirable to make a statement with respect to the administration of the whole department, and in the course of his remarks he spoke of the mineral resources of the country and the development of the gold industry. The hon. member for Davenport confined his observations to the development of another mineral, namely iron ore, and the discussion initiated by the minister and carried on bv the hon. member for Davenport would seem to be appropriate now in view of the fact that the minister, in opening his estimates, discussed the whole subject matter covered by them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item 144 was called.
Quite so.

I have very great respect for the leader of the opposition, but I do not agree with his logic on this occasion. I expressly said that I wished to take advantage of the opening of the discussion of the estimates to give a brief survey of the work of the department. That could have been done if the Speaker had been in the chair and the house were going into committee of supply, but it was the only opportunity I had of making the statement and it was after the item had been called by the chairman. I think it is desirable that the discussion should be kept to the item affected; otherwise, if the logic of the leader of the opposition is sound, we might get into a discussion of parks or water powers or anything else. If we keep to the particular item under discussion we shall probably make greater progress. I have no criticism to offer concerning the hon. member for Davenport, but I think the ruling of the chair is correct. The hon. gentleman's remarks would be entirely appropriate under the next item.

I have no desire to waste time, but when the minister opened his estimates he discussed parks; he mentioned the sum of money spent in Nova Scotia and the sum he proposed to ask for additional parks. He mentioned the sum of money in Prince Edward Island and told of the total

Supply-Mines and Resources
investment in parks. He took mines and spoke of the production in Canada of gold and of baser metals and he also turned to Indian affairs, dividing the expenditures into the sums used for education, medical services and relief. He then turned to the fourth branch, immigration, and said it was stationary. My submission is that it has been customary for ministers-the custom was started in this house by a minister of railways under Sir Wilfrid Laurier-to open their departments to the house, and that precipitated a minor debate with respect to the whole subject matter, giving rise to speeches such as we have heard from the hon. member for Davenport, and to which I understand the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deaeh-man) was about to make an appropriate reply. Surely, once there has been an opening of the department by the calling of an item-and this could not be done until the item was called-the item having been called, and the minister having made a statement, we must take it for granted, unless the chairman stops the minister, that those who follow him should have the same latitude. That is logical, and on that assumption I propose to act.

I shall certainly not get
into a controversy with my right hon. friend, but I believe I did state in my opening remarks that I wished to have the indulgence of the committee to make a general statement.

And I think it is a
very proper thing to do; I compliment the minister upon it.

It might facilitate matters
if this item were allowed to pass. It is a stationary item that has been in the estimates each year, having to do with explosives administration. It covers the expenses of travelling inspectors for the administration of the Explosives Act. If this item is passed, then the way is wide open for the hon. member for Davenport or the hon. member for Huron North or anyone else to take part in the discussion we have been having.

When I hear the minister suggesting that, by the declaration "carried" by the chairman, one can convert a discussion that is otherwise out of order into one that is in order, I think it is time we ceased to quibble about parliamentary procedure. If it will help the minister more readily to accommodate himself to further discussion, I shall not object. The chairman will say "carried" and call the next item, whereupon the member for Huron North will proceed with his speech, after which I may make one myself.

I did not suggest that the
chairman declare the item carried. I suggested to the committee that it might pass the item inasmuch as it is non-contentious, and there would then be an opportunity for hon. members to take part in the discussion of iron deposits.

Item agreed to.
For investigation of mineral resources and deposits; of the mining and metallurgical industries, and of mineral technology; wages, expenses of testing and research laboratories; for publications, English and French, for purchase of books and instruments; for miscellaneous assistance and contingencies; and for investigations by the Dominion Fuel Board, including salaries and all other expenses, $273,000.

Now that the uproar
has ceased, I wish to ask the minister a question as to the difference in cost tO' the public between iron ore produced from Ontario mines and iron ore when imported, as we do import it now, from the United States. Perhaps the minister could give us information in that regard, because I noticed in the speech of the hon. member for Davenport at least the implication that, provided the product were, made in Ontario and made by workers in Canadian iron and with Canadian capital, it did not make very much difference what it cost. He cited the case of Germany and the progress which that country was making in connection with the utilization of its products in the manufacture of certain commodities. I read an interesting article in Harper's Magazine a short time ago. It pointed out that Germany was making rubber at six times the cost of producing it from imported raw rubber. Germany is also making gasoline from coal but at a cost which is four or five times what that commodity would cost if imported. I should not like this parliament, at the suggestion of the hon. member for Davenport, to adopt, such a policy in connection with the administration of affairs in Canada. My reason for that objection is that the great basic industry of agriculture in Canada is not in a condition to bear these burdens, and so I protest against having them imposed upon us at anybody's behest. After all, true economy is to bring your raw material from wherever you can get it and to manufacture the product cheaply, and distribute it to the people at the lowest possible cost, and1 if Canadian capital had thought it worth while to tackle this problem of using Canadian iron I venture to say it would have done so. But we are told that they could do it if you gave them a cent a unit, and an additional cent, or perhaps $2 or $2.50 or whatever it is, per ton of finished ore, for the privilege of producing iron ore in Canada.

Supply-Mines and Resources

My hon. friend wants
help from the dominion government, help from Ontario; both hands are held out.

I have a very tender place in my heart for the agriculturists; anything I can do to help them will be gladly done, and any industry I have been associated with has always been happy to help agriculture. But we never find my hon. friend having a good word to say for labour men or industry; we always find him opposing them; he has nothing good to say for anything except agriculture. I like to help agriculture, but I also think of the 800,000 to 1,000,000 men working in industry.

I should like to say a few words about this important item. I commend the Department of Mines and Resources for the wonderful work it has done, under both the present minister and his predecessor from my neighbouring constituency, Hon. Wesley Gordon. I praised him both personally and publicly when he inaugurated the new policy of sending out geological parties covering practically the whole mineral area of Canada. I was glad to see that last year and this year again this vote is enlarged, as this work has resulted in greatly adding to the knowledge of our country and its mineral formation.
There is one other item for which I beg the government to enlarge its appropriation in the supplementary estimates if at all possible; that is road construction to the newer mining sections. There was a time when northern Ontario and, indeed, the whole of northern Canada was thought to be a barren waste. Northern Ontario has shown not only to Canada but to the whole civilized world that we have there the greatest potential mineral wealth under the sun. There are occasions when, through lack of roads, it has been impossible for some of the new mines to be developed. I should not like to see the government embark upon a policy which would favour certain kinds of wild-catting, which exists to some extent at this time. There may be a little too much speculation at the moment; this is not the time or the place to mention what has been going on, but I know it came to the ears of the department that in some sections the public had been taken for a ride, and I hope the provincial governments more particularly will see that at the present time when we are emerging from the depression the people will not be fleeced. But the responsibility rests upon the federal administration to help road construction in some of
the new mining sections of Canada. I would never be in favour of a policy of spending large sums in sections where there are merely new prospects not proved by actual development. But the fact remains that at present there is a shortage of roads, summer roads and winter roads, but more particularly summer roads, to give access to new mines.
I commend very highly the Department of Mines and Resources for their policy of road construction inaugurated last year, and hope they will find it possible to enlarge it. Perhaps it is not divulging any secret if I say we thought that in northern Ontario, in Temiskaming and Cochrane, and also in northern Quebec, not enough money had been spent. Doubtless the committee have heard some talk about secession from some of our newer sections, but there is nothing in that. At the same time the government must know that as far as northern Ontario and northern Canada are concerned, the mineral industry is a source of great riches and of revenue to both provincial and dominion governments. We do not want all the money to be spent in our own section, but we feel we are entitled to a fair share. The words of praise and commendation which I spoke of Hon. Mr. Gordon apply just as forcibly to the present minister. I was also able very sincerely to compliment the former Minister of Mines of Ontario, Hon. Mr. McCrea, and I feel that the same commendation is due to his successor, Hon. Mr. Leduc. Their work has been of great help in bringing the country out of the depression. Again I express the fervent wish that the federal government will find it possible to spend more money on road construction and also to increase, if possible, the geological parties we have had for the last two years.

If the faith of the minister is anything like that of his predecessor, whose footsteps the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) says he follows, one can suggest that he continue his activities. The explanation which he has given of the consolidation of his department I think merits the approval of this committee. When he suggests that the total saving in personnel is forty-seven in the Ottawa administration, it is important to ascertain what the effect was on what one might call the outside service, about which we may have occasion to speak later. The monetary saving at the moment is apparently over $100,000.
I sympathize with the minister when he refers to the difficulty of dealing with men who have been long in the service. When the Department of the Interior parted with

Supply-Mines and Resources
the natural resources and they were turned over to the provinces, the same difficulties arose and they have not yet been disposed of, for many of those who took pension at that time were not old men, and although orders in council were passed that they should, whenever possible, be afforded opportunity for employment, many of them are still out of the public service. So the difficulty the minister has had to contend with has been considerable.
He divided his observations into four heads. He spoke of the mining industry. May I say to this committee that in the mining industry as such the Dominion of Canada has a very limited interest; for the natural resources belong to the several provinces and not to the federal government. The federal government is no longer trustee for the natural resources of the country except in that part which is not under provincial control. In the Northwest Territories we have still direct control of the mineral wealth. The extent to which, without compensation by way of taxes, the federal government should interest itself in mining ventures is a matter that is open to much discussion. In South Africa 60 per cent of the profits of the great Premier diamond mine was taken by the state. And in the great mining development which goes on in that country 50 per cent of the increased price of gold is paidi to the exchequer; it is less than 50 per cent in some mines, but broadly speaking that is the proportion. Why? Because the nation is responsible, and not the individual provinces, for the increase in the price of gold and the values thus created. That matter is one which has been dealt with by this parliament in a manner without precedent, as was stated in the speech of the Finance minister last year, about which something will be said later. That is the position in South Africa, and in other parts of the king's dominions.
Here we are rendering a very distinct service, and we have it on record that the government do not propose to ask that any contribution be made by the gold mines other than that which they pay as income tax, like other industries. In no other part of the world has gold itself been so looked upon-and why it should be here, is, as the late Rudyard Kipling would say, another story. But I do point out that in dealing with the question of mines and minerals we have some obligations in respect of the unexplored territories, and it is our duty so to conserve those resources as to see that the utmost value enures to the people for whom they

are held in trust. I have no doubt it would be desirable for the dominion government to carry on gold-mining operations in the Northwest Territories. If we should be successful in finding a large deposit of gold, it would enable us to make a payment of our national debt on a scale that otherwise is denied to us, for the only method by which we can hope to make any large payment on that obligation is through some effort of that kind.
The same applies to some of our provinces. That, however, is a matter which involves policy, which need not now be discussed. It must not be forgotten, however, in dealing with our mines and minerals, that the rearmament program of the nations has provided a new market for lead, zinc and copper, and already there are distinct signs that with respect to these metals there is a diminution of demand and an increase of supply. So we must not think that by substituting mining for agriculture we can bring about anything like a restoration of the prosperity of the country. Although it is new wealth it must not be forgotten that it is a failing asset. It is an asset that disappears once and for all, as far as the country itself is concerned, and our only direct receipt of income from these organizations is through the income tax which is paid. I think it was well worth while, as the hon. member for Cochrane has said, to take the steps which were taken by the former Minister of Mines, because at that particular moment this country was in such a position that any increase in its new wealth by methods such as were pursued was greatly to be desired.
I would be loath to believe that of all men the Minister of Mines and Resources had concluded that the mining industry could ever take the place of the agricultural industry in a country such as this. We have conditions here that are very difficult for us to overcome. No man ever realizes that more than when he goes away from home. Climate, the nature of our soil, drought, and matters of that kind make one realize the magnitude of the problem with which our people have to deal. In connection with mining we have the uncertainties to which the minister alluded, as compared with the certainties that prevail on the Rand in South Africa, where they have a completely developed territory and know exactly what can be found, because they have a uniform quality of mineral deposit that is certain to produce results from their operations, which is not quite true in this country at the moment. I think we can reserve further observations

Supply-Mines and Resources
with respect to the mining industry for another occasion, because there will be ample opportunity on one of the other items.
With respect to the Indian problem I confess that I share the minister's view as to its seriousness. We have less than 125,000 Indians in Canada. The population has increased slightly. At one time it was diminishing. It has increased because we have taken such good care of the Indian population, and in my judgment that in itself is to the credit of the Canadian people. The minister has very properly pointed out that the cost seems to be out of all proportion to what reasonably might be expected for the service rendered. I must say that there are two items I have always found it difficult to understand. When estimates were prepared; when one had to consider the question from every angle in days of great depression, I must say that I found it difficult to ascertain by any explanation which could be afforded what value we got for nearly $2,000,000 spent on education. I say that to the minister very frankly, and I agree with every state>-ment he has made. Sometimes I used to fear that there was more interest in getting a per diem allowance with which to enable institutions to continue their work than there was in anything else, because it goes without saying that what the minister has indicated is true. You cannot take boys and girls out of teepees at five and six years of age; put them into residential schools; turn them back to their homes during summer vacation and finally back home after they have completed their education, and expect them to give that account of themselves which one would expect for the moneys expended. Not long ago I heard of a Cambridge graduate who had gone back to his coloured country people in Africa and had reverted to the customs and habits of his tribe, despite all the effort that had been put forth in regard to his education.
I have been close to the problem in various parts of my own province, in connection with the Blood Indians in the southern part of the province; the great tribe that lies just west of my own constituency, the Stonies, the great hunters; the Sarcees, who are not far from Calgary, and that great tribe which has its headquarters near Gleichen. At Macleod, at Morley, at Sarcee and at Gleichen there are four distinct tribes of Indians, and certainly the effort which has been made to preserve their health, to teach them some of the elements of sanitation and to give them some ideas in the way of education has been highly successful in this sense, that they now realize the value of a hospital; they realize the value
of cleanliness and they realize that preventive medicine is more to be preferred than any curative efforts that may be made. We have established doctors upon the reserves; we have built hospitals. In some cases the band funds have been responsible for it; in other cases we have made direct grants, but I do not see how we can lessen those contributions to the well-being of the Indians if we are to maintain the ground that we have won by such great effort. I have seen the change which has taken place since I have been in western Canada. At one time there was a diminution in the Indian population. It is now increasing, and this is a distinct tribute to the efforts that successive governments have made to provide medical services and teach the rudiments of preventive medicine to the Indian population.
I have thought, and perhaps the minister will agree, that in some of these places they might be more successful in their grazing operations. They have raised cattle with indifferent success, for some strange reason. At Gleichen they have a coal mine which they operate with success, and the herds on the Blood reserve are substantial, but whether the operations of the department in that regard can be expanded, I do not know. That is a matter which, I imagine, would engage the attention of the minister and his officials. In connection with the question of education, however, I believe the minister's observations are entirely warranted.
Having exhausted what he had to say with regard to mines and the Indians, the minister turned for a moment to the position in connection with parks. I sometimes think we exaggerate the exact value of the tourist traffic in this country, but that it is a very, very important industry for the purpose of adjusting unfavourable trade balances, as an invisible item, goes without question. When one contemplates the number of people who cross and recross the boundary between this country and the United States and the amount of money that is left here from year to year, it is difficult to estimate it exactly. The parks have played an ever-increasing part in that tourist traffic, and we can afford to spend money in developing them, because that money will produce a real dividend. I am not sure that, as far as the federal government is concerned, the tourist traffic does not give us a greater direct dividend than the moneys we receive, for instance, from one industry at least that has been mentioned. The tourist traffic is so important from the standpoint of an invisible item in our trade relations with other countries that it is difficult to overestimate its value.

Supply-Mines and Resources
With respect to the various park administrations. one can only say that the expenditure of $30,000,000 includes administrative costs as well as capital costs. I hardly think it is fair to include administrative costs, in that sense, but the minister has given them to us only for the purpose of information.
With respect to immigration, I find it difficult to understand why, on the set-up, the services of the deputy minister were dispensed with, for of all the men engaged in the public service from 1930 to this day, no other single man brought about such economies in the public service as did that man. He took the soldier settlement and allied problems connected with loans, and made adjustments such as saved this country more money than is involved in what the minister has now done. Instead of there being forty-seven less people in the employ of the country, the number is very much larger. Before we conclude our discussion of the estimates I shall be able to ascertain what the number is. I remember having noted it, because it struck me as being very large. I do not believe any public servant during my time made a greater contribution to the economic and efficient operation and administration of a department than did the gentleman whose services were dispensed with. However, that is by the way. This does not seem to be the proper place to discuss a question which I believe is very important, namely, whether or not the question of the movement of people into Canada should longer remain stationary. This is a problem which will have to be considered at greater length than I feel disposed to deal with it to-night. But the time is rapidly approaching, if in fact it has not already arrived, when we must realize that the burden of taxation imposed upon our people, and the revenue necessities to meet the charges against our income, have become so very great that an additional number of units is necessary, if we are not to overburden per capita those who are in this dominion.
In addition, there is a larger problem connected with the issue, which need not now be discussed, namely the problem of the waste places of the country being peopled, and the necessity for a readjustment of population in the world. However, this is not a matter with which I shall attempt to deal to-night.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) referred to the iron industry, and I believe the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) also dealt with it. I have only this to say: On more than one occasion I have investigated the matter, and I fancy the minister has done likewise. In Canada
fMr. Bennett.]
we have not, in quantities, iron ore of a quality which would enable us, without importation from some source, to produce the pig iron essential for the production of various kinds of steel. We have iron ore; we have good iron ore, but we have not iron ore located in quantity and quality so as to enable us to deal with the problem in its entirety. Successive ministers have grappled with the problem; successive governments have investigated it, and I regret to say that successive reports have shown just what I have indicated.
At this time, apart from importations from the United States, we import a quantity of ore from Newfoundland. As is known, Newfoundland sells large quantities of ore to Germany. Great as are the German deposits, they still have to rely upon importations. Britain no longer finds herself able to supply her own requirements, and iron ore importations to England come from Sweden, some even from Wabana, Newfoundland, and other parts of the world. The only countries in which I have seen deposits of iron ore located within reasonable distance of the sea in quality and quantity sufficient to produce the highest grade of pig iron and steel, are in South Africa and Australia. The plant at Newcastle, Australia, is one of the four great steel plants of the world: yet we never hear of it. The one in South Africa is far inland, at Pretoria, where they have iron ore situated at some distance from the city, and of a quality which enables them to produce pig iron and steel of the highest grade.
I agree with the observations of the hon. member for Davenport. It is highly desirable that if there is any iron ore in Canada capable of being developed to produce pig iron or steel, we should develop it. I can say to the hon. member, however, that successive governments have made the most extensive investigation, and without the importation of certain qualities of iron ore from other countries we are not in a position to produce the quality of pig iron essential to the development of a great steel industry in this country. I say that with great regret, because it has always been my opinion that the Mesaba range should have been part of Canada on any fit and proper adjustment of boundaries. However, it was decreed otherwise. If one will take the trouble to read with care the life of the late Sir William Van Horne, he will find how nearly the iron ores in that range were to being in possession of a Canadian company rather than a great American company. However, that is not a matter of importance at this time. It is important only because we

Supply-Mines and Resources
rely to a great extent upon another country for our supplies of iron ore to serve our blast furnaces.
The minister has before him a very great opportunity. I can only say to him that I sometimes envy him that opportunity, for in days of great depression the visions and hopes which one had of being able to make reorganizations and adjustments along business lines in some of our departments were never realized. In part, they were realized in the Department of Finance, but outside that they were not. Attacks made when the Department of the Interior was reorganized by reason of resources being passed on to the provinces brought about an almost intolerable position, even in this community, because of the resultant superannuation of so large a number of persons. The very fact the minister has been able to reduce the staff by consolidation only by forty-seven indicates not only the difficulty but also something of the strength of that imponderable force which one has to meet whenever an effort is made to improve the public service of Canada by any reduction in its numbers.
If he will study just one front page of one document, one magazine which came to my hands the other day, he will realize clearly exactly what I mean. If consolidation is to be brought about, we shall all have to help in doing it. There is not a general disposition on the part of all of us to see our friends, as distinct from somebody else's friends, deprived of the employment by which they earn their livelihood. We are all perfectly willing that somebody else's friend should leave his position, but none of us Is prepared to think our own friend should, with the result that a reduction of forty-seven is the net result of the effort the minister has made. I congratulate him upon it. I miss my guess if between now and the time when tired and worn, he surrenders the seals of office, the forty-seven has not been reversed and the figures show plus, not minus.

I shall try to be brief, but I should like to commend the minister for his hearty cooperation in helping to develop the north country. I believe it is the duty of members from mining constituencies to make themselves familiar with everything in those constituencies. I found that while I visited mines in other places I was not familiar with those of my own constituency. When I got off the train I made a trip of twenty miles in to a mine. May I say it took five and a half hours to go in and five hours to come out. Perhaps the truck ran better on the way home. I think we could have walked much faster. I
thought that mine was being forced to operate under unfair conditions. I got into touch with the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar); he got into touch with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and with the provincial members, and we were finally able to get $4,500 for the improvement of the road into that mine.
I answer the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) with some fear and trembling, and I congratulate the minister upon the progress he has made in taking care of the Indians. I visited three bands of Indians north of lake Nipigon and I found there something which I did not think existed in Canada, that is, cooperation being practised on a very large scale. I saw the finest patch of potatoes I have seen since I left the Emerald Isle. This patch was thirty acres in extent and the potatoes were all large and clean. These boys knew how to raise, plant and cultivate the potatoes. I think our Indians should be taught how to live as well as how to make a living. With the exception of two old people, not one person in those bands was receiving relief. I think the minister should be commended for the progressiveness and the educational features of the Indian affairs branch.

I should like to say a word or two about this very important item. I consider it to be one of the most important to be considered by the committee of supply. It deals with mining and metallurgy, with the Dominion Fuel Board and all that sort of thing. I must say that there is only a skeleton department to handle this very important phase of the natural resources of Canada. There has been a steady increase in the number of students enrolling at McGill, Toronto, Queens and the other Canadian universities for courses in mining and metallurgy. We should compare this item for this very important work with the items voted in the United States. There may be concurrent jurisdiction as between the dominion and the provinces, but I do not think it goes far enough. There is no coordination, and there should be.
The universities have been coming to this parliament for many years but we are doing nothing for them. Three years ago the Canadian Council of Mining and Metallurgy met in Ottawa. This organization is composed of the great men in this great profession. Many of these men are graduates of the universities of this country. We should consider the work being done along these lines in Germany. Many students who are in thieir third and fourth year of practical science spent last summer working at pick

Supply-Mines and Resources
and shovel jobs in the mines. These students should be taken care of the way they are taken care of in Germany; they should be put to work making a scientific study of these problems. We are absolutely behind the times. We are voting only three-quarters of a million dollars to provide merely a skeleton department to handle this very important work. This is the same sort of department as we have in connection with health matters.
If the government want to do something to bring about better times, they should take note of what is being done in some of the large universities of the world. In those universities every provision is being made for the advanced study of these great problems. The government would derive untold revenue if they provided further assistance along these lines. Many of our great engineers have gone to South America, South Africa and Australia. The number of students enrolling for these courses has increased in recent years. At one time civil engineering, chemistry and other courses used to be popular, but now it is mining and metallurgy. The former government voted about $2,000,000 in order that surveys might be undertaken throughout the country. This was only a drop in the bucket to what could be done.
The latter part of the item deals with the Dominion Fuel Board. This board does very good work. As all members know, this is one of the coldest countries in the world. We have from seven to eight months of cold weather and we are still dependent upon American supplies of coal. We are not doing very much to provide the working classes of this country with cheaper fuel. The two inquiries which have been held into the matter of fuel supply did not touch the national fuel problem. Ten or twelve years ago this house adopted a national fuel policy. Under this policy all the fuel used in Canada would be British mined, that is, mined in England, Wales, Nova Scotia or Alberta. In answer to a question the other day the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) said that they could not give the movement of coal from the mari-times to the head of the lakes. There is a booklet issued by the Department of Labour containing fifteen or twenty tables which deal with this fuel problem and its relation to the work of the fuel board. Are we going to be dependent forever upon the United States? Why do we not develop our own fuel supply?
Why do we not utilize the latent talent now lying idle in the universities of this country? The last commission's report shows that they did nothing and they did it well. I think the work of this Dominion Fuel Board should be expanded. The universities should be given

the opportunity of cooperating with the government. We should develop a policy of Canada for Canadians. The engineers who took part in the great hydro development were all graduates of Toronto, McGill, Queens and other Canadian universities. I can see very little hope in this item for our universities. What we should be doing is voting several million dollars to provide for surveys all over the country which would utilize every student in our universities. This opportunity should be given to the poorer students who are dependent upon what they can earn at such work to pay their fees. I hope in the not too distant future we shall wake up in this dominion. We are miles behind the times. I direct the attention of the committee to what is being done in Germany and also in Wales. There are very good men connected with this Dominion Fuel Board, but their hands are tied and they can do nothing. I commend the minister and his officials for the good work done already, but much better work can be done if an opportunity is given to these men to do it.
The deputy minister has a national reputation. and I want to compliment him upon all he has done for the mining industry. If we are to increase the wealth of this country and have a greater output from our mines, I plead with the government to utilize students during the summer time so that when they graduate they will not leave their country but will stay here and be a credit to Canada after all the toil and labour which they and their parents have put into their training.

Mr. Chairman, coming from a mining constituency I should like to say a few words to the hon. minister (Mr. Crerar).
For the past few years, as he knows, we have had geological surveys coming into the Yukon, and they have done wonderful work. I believe it has been intimated that in the future men are to do some prospecting for the government. I hope that is so. We have an enormous territory covering over 200,000 square miles, and we export only gold, silver, copper, zinc, lead and a few other metals. There are some coal mines in that country, but so far the coal has not been of a quality that we could use comfortably.
The gold mines have been far more valuable in the last few years because of the rise in the price of gold to $35. In Dawson district one company has operated very largely, and it did very much better in the past year than in previous years. I spoke of their camps last year. This summer when I went north I found that new camps were built, and that the men were far better looked after than in all the years I have been north. At one of

the camps the superintendent told me it was only a temporary camp. I looked at him when he told me it was only a temporary camp because to my certain knowledge it has been a temporary camp for seven years, and is likely to be so for another seven years unless somebody gets after it. But generally the camps have been improved, and that part of the country is doing infinitely better.
They have not done what I feel they should do with regard to their hours of labour. They work their men ten and twelve hours a day, and I do not believe a man can work properly at mining for ten and twelve hours a day. In the silver mining camp, at Tread-well-Y'ukon, the men work eight hours a day.
The Mayo district is dependent almost entirely upon the output of silver. In the early twenties when silver went to SI.38, a new high, the district was a beehive of industry ; we were fortunate in having in charge of the Treadwell-Yukon mine a mining engineer who was a worker himself, an ambitious man, and he did the best he could for that part of the country. In 1925-26 silver went down to 58 cents, and in 1928-29 to a low price of from 25 to 27 cents, and the mines were closed down and hundreds of miners were thrown out of work.
The silver mining industry is a difficult industry in that country because the ore must be sacked. At first it was raw-hided, taken fifty miles to the river bank, stored on the river bank during the summer, then put on barges and steamers and taken down to Stewart on the Yukon river, then moved up river to White Horse, and from White Horse transferred to barge and steamer, then put on flat cars and taken to tidewater at Skag-way and brought out, and again transferred from steamer to train. It is pretty difficult when one has to carry ore in that way. At the Treadwell mine in Juneau, the ore can be worked at a profit of from 90 cents to 82 a ton, but in the Yukon there is only a very small profit when silver is 40 cents an ounce. That I think the minister can readily understand when he knows what our transportation system is.
Owing to the very high water we had this summer there was trouble along both the Yukon and Stewart rivers. Several barges were lost; some ore was lost; other ore had to be resaeked and transferred, not once but several times. If it had not been for the ore stacked on the shore at Mayo, the town would have been almost washed out. In that town there were only three buildings which were not under water: the government liquor store, of course, and this was a blessing in a way;
the Roman Catholic church and the Anglican church. The one person in the town of Mayo who seemed to have a sense of impending disaster was a Cbeechako, a newcomer who warned people that the river was going higher. The manager of the local bank moved out the bank books and valuables and stored them in the tower of the Catholic church, and the bank furniture was the only furniture that was saved.
I hardly intended to go into all this detail to-night, but I did want to speak of it and convey a very hearty invitation to the minister to come to the Yukon and see for himself what we need. I believe the people in the Mayo district would be more than pleased if he did so and it is almost a necessity for them to have a mining engineer settle in that country for at least one year. He could help our prospectors, help the men who have the silver mines, and do a great deal of work for us.
I see it is now eleven o'clock, and with the permission of the Chair I should like to resume when this item comes up again. I thank you.
